# heki

> Experimental static checker for Python that tracks side effects and mutations across function calls.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/

# heki

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/heki-banner.png" alt="heki: a snake in front of a brick wall" width="600">
</p>

🧱 heki (壁, Japanese for "wall") is a static checker for Python, written in Rust. It tracks side
effects and mutations across function calls.

It catches blocking I/O in `async` code, database queries and HTTP clients in loops, and
quadratic loops. You can also add rules in `pyproject.toml` to restrict which functions may
mutate state or reach I/O.

![heki check in a terminal: EFF101 reports a blocking call two helpers below an async def, and EFF103 a database query one helper below a loop, each with its call chain](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/assets/example-check.svg)

By default, heki shows only *exact* reports: reports of a certified rule, built only from facts
heki established. To certify a rule, two reviewers check by hand every exact report it makes on
the development corpus (378 packages and 30.75 million lines, plus packages added for rules with
few reports), and one run on a frozen holdout of 100 packages is checked too. Neither may hold a
false claim. `EFF101` and `EFF103`, the rules of the two examples below, had 287 and 103 reports
on the corpus and 152 and 122 on the holdout, none false.
[Rule precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications) lists every certified rule.

*Heuristic* reports can be wrong about the code. They are opt-in (`heki check --heuristic`), and
every output labels them.

<p>
  <a class="md-button md-button--primary" href="getting-started/">Getting Started</a>
  <a class="md-button" href="rules/">Rules</a>
  <a class="md-button" href="configuration/">Configuration</a>
</p>

[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/heki)](https://pypi.org/project/heki/)
[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/heki)](https://pypi.org/project/heki/)
[![CI](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/LICENSE)

⚡ Try it in your project's root, without installing: `uvx heki check`

---

### A blocking call two helpers below an `async def`

```python
# app/users.py
import requests

def fetch_name(user_id: int) -> str:
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}", timeout=5).text

def load_user(user_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"id": str(user_id), "name": fetch_name(user_id)}
```

```python
# app/api.py
from app.users import load_user

async def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    return load_user(user_id)
```

```console
$ heki check
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 (async-blocking-call) [warning] `app.users.load_user` always runs the waiting call `requests.get` on the event loop (2 calls down, on every path)
  |
5 |     return load_user(user_id)
  |            ^
  = related: app/api.py:5:12: `get_user` calls `app.users.load_user`
  = related: app/users.py:8:41: `load_user` calls `app.users.fetch_name`
  = related: app/users.py:5:12: `fetch_name` calls `requests.get`
  = help: offload it with `asyncio.to_thread`, or use an async client

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 2 file(s).
note: 5 heuristic rule(s) are off; enable them with `--heuristic` or `lint.heuristic = true`
```

### A query one helper below a loop

```python
# app/orders.py
import sqlite3

def customer_name(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, customer_id: int) -> str:
    cursor.execute("SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = ?", (customer_id,))
    return str(cursor.fetchone()[0])

def order_summaries(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, orders: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> list[str]:
    lines: list[str] = []
    for order_id, customer_id in orders:
        lines.append(f"#{order_id} {customer_name(cursor, customer_id)}")
    return lines
```

```console
$ heki check
app/orders.py:11:37: EFF103 (loop-db-query) [warning] every iteration over parameter `orders` sends a database statement: `sqlite3.Cursor.execute` (through `app.orders.customer_name`)
   |
11 |         lines.append(f"#{order_id} {customer_name(cursor, customer_id)}")
   |                                     ^
  = related: app/orders.py:11:37: `order_summaries` calls `app.orders.customer_name`
  = related: app/orders.py:5:5: `customer_name` calls `sqlite3.Cursor.execute`
  = help: batch the queries, or load the data once before the loop

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 1 file(s).
note: 5 heuristic rule(s) are off; enable them with `--heuristic` or `lint.heuristic = true`
```

Ruff, ty, Pyrefly, pyright, and mypy report nothing for either example with their default settings.

### What a first run shows

Run `uvx heki check` (or `heki check` once [installed](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/installation/)) in the directory with
`pyproject.toml`:

- An error reports a bug: a wrong result, an exception, a lost update, a deadlock, or a broken
  contract. A warning reports slower code, like the two above, or a bug that is rarely harmful.
- Warnings are printed and do not fail the run (exit code 0). Errors fail it (exit code 1).
  [`--fail-on warning`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint)
  (`lint.fail-on = "warning"`) makes warnings fail it too.
- A note at the end says how many heuristic rules were left off; `--heuristic` runs them.

### Your own conventions, too

The checks above need no configuration: `EFF101` and `EFF103` are exact and run by default.
The rules of your own project, which you keep today by review, by AST scripts, or by run-time
guards in tests, can be added as a few lines of [configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/):

```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "order-store"
targets = ["app.models.Order.items"]
allowed-writers = ["app.store.*"]
```

heki follows aliases, helpers, and subclasses, with no decorators and nothing running at run
time. The other contracts are `read-owners`, `call-owners`, `readonly-returns`, `invalidation`,
and `effect-boundaries`.

!!! warning "Experimental"

    The exact rules are certified, but heki is still under active development: rules,
    configuration keys, diagnostics, and output formats can change between releases without a
    deprecation period. Try it on your code and report what it gets wrong.

## ✨ Why heki?

Types say what values are; heki checks what code does:

- **Aliases and in-place changes:** which objects a function changes, through any alias, helper,
  or subclass.
- **Contracts:** who may write, read, or call what, and which code may reach I/O.
- **Proven rewrites:** quadratic patterns are rewritten only when the rewrite is proven, not
  guessed.

### What code does, not what types it has

These rules are exact and run by default. Each report shows the chain of calls that leads to it.

| What goes wrong | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| A blocking call that a call in an `async def` always runs, several helpers below | [`EFF101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/) |
| A database statement on every iteration of a loop over data | [`EFF103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/) |
| A `Sequence` / `Mapping` argument changed in place by a helper | [`MUT110`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/) |
| A list, dict, or set that an `lru_cache` / `cache` function returned, changed in place | [`MUT114`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/) |
| A DataFrame or array concatenated with itself on every loop iteration | [`DATA101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/) |
| A quadratic list, dict, set, bytes, or queue pattern | `OPT101`-`OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT113`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130` ([fixes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/)) |

The other rules are heuristic or opt-in, and the [contract](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) rules run
once you declare a contract: see [Rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) and [Rule precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

### A safety net for reviews and coding agents

- The [language server](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/) checks while you edit and re-checks only what an edit can affect.
- [`heki snapshot`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103) records what each public function does, and `MUT103` reports a function that gained an
  effect, which a diff does not show.
- [Coding agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/) get the same checks as JSON, and an
  [Agent Skill](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental) teaches them the workflow.

### Fast, quiet, and easy to adopt

- A 100,000-line project is checked in a few seconds.
- A report needs evidence: when heki cannot tell, [it stays quiet](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#when-heki-cannot-tell).
- Configuration, suppression comments, and output formats follow Ruff, and a [baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) fails CI
  only on new findings.

## 🔓 What Python leaves open

| What Python leaves open | What other languages enforce | What heki checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any code can change any object it reaches | ownership and borrowing (Rust), `const` / `readonly` | read-only parameters and fields changed through helpers (`MUT110`, `MUT108`); `write-owners` / `read-owners` contracts (`MUT201`, `MUT203`) |
| A signature does not say what a function does | effect types, `IO` in the type (Haskell) | blocking calls reached from `async def`, and clients and queries in loops (`EFF101`–`EFF103`); `effect-boundaries` (`EFF201`); effect snapshots (`MUT103`) |
| Shared mutable objects hide changes | value semantics, immutability by default | stale cached properties and hashes (`MUT101`, `MUT107`); changed shared return values (`MUT114`, `MUT202`); writes an `invalidation` contract must announce (`MUT109`) |
| Dynamic dispatch blocks optimizations | static types let a compiler prove a rewrite | quadratic patterns (`OPT`), rewritten only when proven under CPython's semantics |

## 🔍 How heki differs

The difference is the model, not reaching across files: type checkers already follow types
across modules. heki models effects and aliases, what code does:

| Tool | Models | heki adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ruff | syntax and style | the effects behind a call: a blocking call, a query, or a write, wherever it happens |
| ty, Pyrefly, pyright, mypy | declared types | in-place changes, through aliases and helpers, to `frozen`, `ReadOnly`, and `Final` fields and to `Sequence` / `Mapping` arguments |
| tach, import-linter | which modules may import which | which functions write or read a field, call a function, or reach I/O |

Their stricter settings do not close the gap. The second example above is fully annotated and
passes Ruff's annotation rules (`ANN`), `mypy --strict`, pyright's strict mode, and Pyrefly's
`strict` preset, yet it sends one query per order: the types are right, and what the code does
is slow.

heki leaves to these tools what they cover, and keeps doing so as they grow: use it next to them.

## 🔧 Rewrites proven under CPython's semantics

The `OPT` rules find quadratic list, dict, set, bytes, and queue patterns. `heki check --fix`
rewrites one only when it proves that the program behaves the same:

- it trusts no type annotation (a subclass can override `__add__`);
- any other reference to the object blocks an in-place update;
- evaluation order and exceptions are kept;
- builtins count only while the module does not rebind them.

A `collections.deque` rewrite also updates the annotation and adds the import:

```console
$ heki check --diff --include-size-dependent jobs.py
--- a/jobs.py
+++ b/jobs.py
@@ -1,11 +1,12 @@
 """Job queue."""
 
+import collections
 import os
 
 
 def drain(jobs: list[int]) -> int:
-    queue: list[int] = list(jobs)
+    queue: collections.deque[int] = collections.deque(list(jobs))
     total = 0
     while queue:
-        total += queue.pop(0)
+        total += queue.popleft()
     return total
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

`--fix` alone applies the rewrites that are faster for every input (`OPT101`, `OPT102`); a
size-dependent one like this needs `--include-size-dependent`.

The scope analysis is checked against CPython's `symtable` on 3.11 to 3.15, and adversarial
programs that break a naive rewrite must all be blocked on CPython. When a proof fails, the
report names the missing obligation instead of offering a fix. See [Fixes and safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/).

- ⚙️ [Configure](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/) rule selection, contracts, and the Python version.
- 📏 Browse the [42 rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/), and see [how precise each one is](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## 📛 Name

*heki* is 壁, "wall", in its Sino-Japanese (*on*) reading, the one used in compounds such as
防火壁 (*bōkaheki*, "firewall"). On its own the character is usually read *kabe*.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/

# Scope and Limitations

This page says what heki checks, what it leaves to other tools, where its knowledge comes from,
and what it does when it cannot tell.

## Where heki fits

| Tool | Looks at | Example |
| ---- | -------- | ------- |
| A linter such as [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) | Syntax and style, one file at a time | `time.sleep()` written directly in an `async def`; a discarded `asyncio.create_task(...)` |
| A type checker such as [ty](https://github.com/astral-sh/ty) | Whether values match their declared types | a `str` passed where an `int` is expected |
| An import-graph checker such as [tach](https://github.com/gauge-sh/tach) or [import-linter](https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter) | Which modules may import which | `app.api` importing `app.db` when the declared layers forbid it |
| heki | What code does, not what types it has: effects and aliases, through any number of calls | an `async def` that reaches `requests.get` three helpers away; a model field written outside the store that owns it; an attribute `__hash__` reads changing after the object went into a `set` |

The difference is the model, not reaching across files: heki models effects and aliases, and
leaves syntax, types, and imports to the tools that model them, also as they grow. Where another
tool covers part of a case, heki keeps the rest: Ruff's `RUF006` reports discarded tasks, so
`EFF107` reports only the tasks bound to a variable.

### Clean for Ruff, ty, and tach; broken all the same

```python
# app/clients.py
import requests


def fetch_json(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url, timeout=5).json()


# app/users.py
from app.clients import fetch_json


def load_profile(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return fetch_json(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")


def load_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return {"id": user_id, **load_profile(user_id)}


# app/api.py
from app.users import load_user


async def handler(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return load_user(user_id)  # blocks the event loop three calls down
```

```python
# app/models.py: only `Store.*` may write `Model.fields` (a write-owners contract)
class Model:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.fields: list[str] = []


class Store:
    def add_field(self, model: Model, name: str) -> None:
        model.fields.append(name)


def add_default(fields: list[str]) -> None:
    fields.append("id")


def parse(model: Model) -> None:
    fields = model.fields
    add_default(fields)  # changes `Model.fields` behind the store's back
```

```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "model-store"
targets = ["Model.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
```

Each of these passes, because each tool sees one step:

| Command | Sees | Does not see |
| ------- | ---- | ------------ |
| `ruff check --select ASYNC,B,RUF,PERF,PL,SIM,FURB,S` | `requests.get` only when it is written in the `async def` itself | the call three helpers down |
| `ty check` | a `list[str]` passed where a `list[str]` is expected | that `add_default` changes `Model.fields` |
| `tach check` (with `app.api` → `app.users` → `app.clients` declared) | `app.api` importing `app.users`, which is allowed | what `load_user` does |

heki follows the call into `load_user` and the alias into `add_default`:

```console
$ heki check --output-format concise
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 `app.users.load_user` always runs the waiting call `requests.get` on the event loop (3 calls down, on every path)
app/models.py:17:5: MUT201 [heuristic] `parse` writes `Model.fields` (indirect_helper) via `app.models.add_default` outside the write owners of `model-store`
Found 2 diagnostic(s) in 4 file(s).
note: 5 heuristic rule(s) are off; enable them with `--heuristic` or `lint.heuristic = true`
```

## Where heki pays off

| Code | What heki finds |
| ---- | --------------- |
| Async services, and web or database code written in layers of helpers | blocking calls that reach the event loop, clients and queries created inside loops (N+1), I/O while a lock or a transaction is held |
| Large code bases that protect shared state by convention, review, or their own checkers | contract violations, followed through aliases, helpers, and subclasses |
| Loops over growing collections | proven-safe rewrites and suggestions for quadratic patterns |

In small scripts, or code that is mostly synchronous and self-contained, a linter and a type
checker cover most of what matters, and heki reports little.

## What heki does not do

| Check | Use instead |
| ----- | ----------- |
| Style, formatting, and syntax | a linter such as Ruff |
| Type errors | a type checker such as ty |
| Import layering and import cycles | [tach](https://github.com/gauge-sh/tach) or [import-linter](https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter), and Python 3.15's `lazy import` |
| Dead code and duplicated code | Ruff or [vulture](https://github.com/jendrikseipp/vulture) |
| Constant-factor micro-optimizations, such as hoisting `re.compile` | no heki rule |

- heki does not change your code's shape: it adds no decorators, contract types, or runtime
  checks, and it does not compile or rewrite code at build time.
- heki never runs or instruments your program. `--profile` only reads a profile you recorded
  yourself.

## Where heki's knowledge comes from

| Source | What it tells heki | Extend it with |
| ------ | ------------------ | -------------- |
| Its own analysis | an SSA form of every function; aliases (copies, attributes, and the iterators and views derived from an object); what each function mutates and which effects it reaches, propagated over the project's call graph until nothing changes | - |
| A catalog of library behavior | `requests.get` blocks on the network; `asyncio.to_thread(fn)` and `@sync_to_async` run a function on another thread; `logging` calls are never reported; `sqlite3.connect()` returns a `Connection`; `threading.Lock` is a synchronous lock | [`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem) |
| Contracts you declare | who may write, read, or call (`write-owners`, `read-owners`, `call-owners`); which returned objects are shared (`readonly-returns`); which changes must be announced (`invalidation`); which functions must not reach I/O or writes (`effect-boundaries`) | [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) in the configuration |
| Type annotations, as hints only | which class an object has and which method a call reaches: `session: Session` makes `session.execute(...)` a database call | annotations in your code |

- heki does not analyze the source of the standard library or of installed packages: the
  catalog declares their effects.
- Contracts need no decorators, no special types, and nothing at run time.
- The checking rules (`MUT`, `EFF`, `DATA`, `OPT112`, `OPT113`) use annotations. The rewriting
  rules never read them, because a subclass can override any method (see
  [Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#what-a-fix-must-prove)).

### How a call is resolved

heki looks for the callee in this order:

1. local constructors and imports;
2. annotations;
3. attributes assigned in `__init__`;
4. the class hierarchy, up to eight overriding methods.

It also follows container item types (`list[Model]`), return annotations along the MRO,
`isinstance` narrowing, unions of up to three classes, and project `Protocol`s.

## When heki cannot tell

A rewrite and an exact report make the same choice when information is missing, in opposite
directions; a heuristic report makes it only for some premises:

| | A rewrite (`OPT` fix) | An exact report | A heuristic report |
| - | --------------------- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| Needs | a proof | every premise of its claim established | evidence, with some premises open |
| What heki cannot see | counts as shared and blocks the fix | stops the report | stops it for an unresolved call; does not stop it for the premises its rule page marks open |
| What you get | the diagnostic names the failed obligation: `[not auto-fixable: ...]` | no report: a missed finding, never a guess | a report labelled `heuristic`, which can be wrong about the code |

Each rule page lists the premises of its claim under "What a report states", and which of them
a heuristic report may not have established ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).

A report that crosses functions shows its call chain as related locations. A call heki cannot
resolve is not followed:

- a value of type `Any`, or an unannotated parameter;
- a method name computed at run time;
- a call with more than eight possible overrides;
- a method no project class along a class's MRO defines, when a base of the class is a value
  heki cannot name where its class statement runs (`class Derived(base)` with `base` a
  parameter, a local, or a call's result), which may define it; such a class is no subclass of
  any project class either;
- a function outside the checked files that the catalog does not list.

Two more cases stay quiet by design:

- A branch the caller's arguments switch off is not followed: `load(name, cache=False)` does not
  reach the request under `if cache:`.
- A client or query created only while an attribute is unset counts once per object, not once
  per loop iteration, and so does a `functools.cached_property` getter; one created only while
  a module global or a local variable the loop carries is unset (or a first-iteration flag
  holds), or right before the loop ends (`break`, `return`, `raise`), counts once per loop.
- A blocking wait on a `concurrent.futures.Future` known to be done (`if f.done():`, after
  `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)`) returns at once.
- `queue.Queue.put` waits only on a queue known to be bounded: a positive `maxsize` on some
  path, every path known. A `put` on a queue heki cannot follow to where it is built is not
  reported.

A file that cannot be read or does not parse is reported (exit code 2), and every other file is
checked as usual. A file that does not parse cannot run either, so heki assumes nothing it would
do: it calls nothing, defines no subclass, and patches no `builtins`. Its module still owns its
name: `import requests` reaches a project's own `requests.py`, and while that file does not
parse, the names under it resolve to nothing, never to the `requests` of the catalog.

A function whose model would pass its size budget (4 units per byte of its source, at most
50,000; real code stays below one unit per byte) is left unmodeled: heki rewrites nothing in it
and treats its body as one call it cannot resolve. `heki assumptions` lists it with the hazard
`unmodeled`. A function whose proof state (a fact per variable per block) would pass 8 cells per
byte of its source, at most 250,000, gets no `OPT` finding: heki does not try to prove a rewrite
in it. A function whose lazy initializations (the blocks each covers, and the walks that find
them) would take more than 8 cells per byte of its source, at most 250,000, has none of them
recognized: in a heuristic report its clients and queries count as made on every iteration,
and an exact report stops there.

A heuristic report goes the other way for the premises its rule page marks open: a branch heki
cannot decide counts as taken, a loop in which heki cannot show that a call runs once counts as
running it on every iteration, and a size heki cannot bound counts as data-sized (the code does
not fix it at 16 items or fewer). A loop over a list that is small by its nature (the columns of
a table, a handful of options) is reported: the report states a loop whose size the code does
not bound, and whether the loop is slow is the harm, which the rule cannot see. When an open
premise is false (a bound the code states that heki does not read, a call that cannot run on
every iteration), the report is wrong about the code, which is why it is heuristic. An exact
report never claims a size: it names the input a loop steps through.

Missed findings close as heki learns more:

| heki lacks | Add |
| ---------- | --- |
| the class of a value | an annotation |
| your blocking or offloading APIs | an entry in [`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem) |
| the rules of your shared state | a [contract](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) |

## Known limitations

### Dynamic names

`setattr(obj, "fields", v)`, `getattr(obj, "fields")`, `getattr(obj, "method")(...)`, and
`obj.__dict__["fields"]`:

- **Followed** when the name is a constant: a literal, a module-level `Final` string
  (`KEY: Final = "_key"`), also when imported, re-exported, or bound to another `Final` name, a
  module-level string bound once in its module, or a class constant declared `ClassVar` or
  `Final` and bound once (`Model.KEY`, `self.KEY`, `cls.KEY`).
- **Not followed** for a module-level name without `Final` that another module rebinds or deletes,
  one bound in a loop or before a star import that may rebind it, a class constant stored on its
  class or an instance outside the class body (`Model.KEY = "x"`; from another module, only one
  without `Final`), a class constant a subclass defines again, is given its own value
  (`Child.KEY = "x"`), or inherits first from another base it lists before the class
  (`class Child(Other, Model)`; read on that subclass, or on an instance or `cls` that may be one),
  a `Final` field of a dataclass or of a class a `dataclass_transform` builds read on an instance
  (`Keys("x").KEY` is `"x"`), or on a class object whose default a class with `slots=True` or built
  by a transform replaces, or a computed name.
- `setattr` and `object.__setattr__` are followed through a module-level name bound once to them
  (`_set = object.__setattr__`), and `getattr(obj, "fields")` is `obj.fields` itself: changing
  what it returns changes the attribute's object.
- `vars(obj)` (the builtin, not a name shadowing it) is `obj.__dict__`: an entry stored, deleted,
  set by a container method, or updated in place (`vars(obj) |= other`, also on
  `obj.__dict__`) through either is a write of the attribute it names.
- A write-owners contract sees a container change through what a method or a property returns
  when it returns the attribute itself on every `return` (`node.members().append(x)` with
  `return self.items`) and every class the object may be runs it. A `cached_property` hands out
  nothing: what the instance keeps can be replaced.
- A `write-owners` contract with `unresolved = "report"` reports the writes heki cannot tie to a
  class ([`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/)).

### Objects without a known class

- Reads and writes through `Any` or unannotated parameters are not tied to a class, so contracts
  on that class do not see them. A contract with `unresolved = "report"` reports them by name:
  writes under [`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/), reads under
  [`MUT206`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/), and method calls under
  [`MUT207`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/).
- A write in an unannotated helper is still found where a caller passes it an object of a known
  class. A read is not.
- Not typed: values declared `Any`, generics substituted through `TypeVar`s, and calls of
  `type[C]` attributes.

### Names the catalog does not list

Catalog lookups are exact. These contribute no effect until you add them with
[`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem):

- a class reached through another public name: `from sqlalchemy import Engine` for
  `sqlalchemy.engine.Engine`, `redis.StrictRedis` for `redis.Redis`;
- a method the catalog does not list;
- objects reached through subscripts or framework attributes, which have no known class:
  `client["app"]["users"]`, Django's `Model.objects`.

### Properties

- **Followed:** reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` of a project class runs its
  getter. Its effects, writes, and the attributes it reads count for the reader, also through
  base classes, overriding subclasses, and `super()`. The getter's return annotation types the
  value read.
- **Not followed:** a property that also defines a setter or deleter (`@x.setter`), and
  `x = property(get_x)`.

### Read-only types

- `MUT110` follows `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `ReadOnly` parameters into the helpers they are
  handed to, any number of calls deep. A helper parameter annotated with a mutable type is left
  to the type checker, and a container inside the argument does not count.
- `MUT108` (opt-in) follows frozen dataclasses, `NamedTuple`s, classes that a
  `dataclass_transform(frozen_default=True)` in the checked files builds, `Final` / `ReadOnly`
  attributes, and `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys. It does not see the transforms of installed
  packages (attrs, Pydantic), and an instance the function constructs itself counts as under
  construction.

### Generators and coroutines

A generator's body runs where it is iterated:

| Followed | Not followed |
| -------- | ------------ |
| a `for` loop or a comprehension | a generator handed to anything else: `StreamingResponse(rows())`, a container |
| unpacking, `yield from` | a generator only stepped with `next()` |
| a consuming call: `list(...)`, `"".join(...)`, `items.extend(...)` | a generator unpacked into a call: `f(*rows())` |
| a lazy wrapper iterated there: `enumerate(...)` | |
| a project function iterating it | |

- A generator a function returns runs where its caller iterates it.
- A generator expression counts where it is written.
- A coroutine runs where it is awaited; one only scheduled (`asyncio.create_task`) is checked on
  its own.
- Iterating an object runs its class's `__iter__` only for classes the catalog lists (a
  SQLAlchemy `Query`). The `__iter__` methods of project classes are not followed.

### Guards

- **Followed:** a test of the function's own input: truthiness, `is None`, `isinstance` with
  builtin classes, the `io` classes, or `os.PathLike`, or `hasattr` with a string literal, also
  after the function rebinds the input on some paths (`if buf is None: buf = StringIO()`).
- **Decided by:** constants, displays and comprehensions, `io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` objects
  the caller constructs, and the literal defaults of omitted parameters (`hasattr` only for the
  methods of the file protocol: `read`, `write`, `close`, ...); not by an f-string, the result of
  another call, or an instance of a subclass.
- **Not followed:** `a or b` (no guard on either value), and `isinstance` with project classes or
  annotated types.
- A lazy initialization needs a direct test and the store in the function itself: a test in a
  caller of the method that stores, a test combined with `or` / `and`, and memos keyed by an
  argument (`@lru_cache`, a dict) are not followed.
- A future is known to be done only through `f.done()` and `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)`, not
  through an event or another future its done callback sets.
- A queue is known to be bounded through local variables, the attributes its class family's own
  bodies and methods store, module globals, and parameters whose project callers decide (a
  helper's at each call, an `async def`'s by the join of every caller). Not followed: stores into
  an attribute from outside the class family, a `maxsize` checked to be positive but not known,
  an integer constant imported from another module or passed on through a parameter other than
  a literal default, and a queue whose function has no project caller.
- `EFF201` does not use guards.
- An object a factory function returns counts as obtained once, like a pooled connection.

### Separate scopes

- Generator expressions and lambdas are analyzed as functions of their own:
  `next(b for b in bs if b.id == a.id)` inside a loop is not reported as a nested-loop join.
- Two lambdas in one function share the qualified name `f.<locals>.<lambda>`, so heki may
  attribute one lambda's effects to a call of the other:

```python
import requests


async def handler(url: str) -> int:
    fetch = lambda: requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    size = lambda: len(url)
    return size()  # reported as reaching `requests.get` (EFF101)
```

### Metaprogramming and frameworks

`__getattr__` proxies, metaclasses, classes created at run time, and framework machinery
(validators, ORM lazy loading, dependency injection) are not modeled. heki has no
framework-specific rules.

### The target Python version

Results follow [`target-version`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings), which defaults to the
oldest version `requires-python` admits.

- From Python 3.12, list, set, and dict comprehensions run in the enclosing function (PEP 709): a
  comprehension inside a loop can be reported for `py312` and not for `py311`.
- From Python 3.14, annotations are evaluated lazily in `__annotate__` scopes (PEP 649).
- The parser reads Python 3.15 syntax for every target version: `lazy import` (PEP 810) is a lazy
  import also in code for an older version.
- Syntax newer than the target version is analyzed, not reported: that is Ruff's check.

### Source encodings

heki reads the encoding a PEP 263 declaration names: UTF-8 (with or without a BOM), Latin-1, and
ASCII. A file declaring any other encoding is reported as an error and not checked. Unlike a file
that does not parse, such a file runs: what it defines and does stays unknown to the analysis of
the other files.

### Sizes known only at run time

Whether a collection is small is decided from the code: a list whose size depends on the
input counts as large, even when it always holds three items. The rules this affects are marked size-dependent;
[Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#when-the-size-is-fixed) lists what counts as a fixed size.

### Callers outside the checked files

Contracts reason about the callers heki sees: a private helper hands its reports to its callers,
and a function called only from allowed writers is not reported. Code outside the run, such as
tests left out of it, is not known.

## How a rule gets into heki

heki only takes checks that need what it can prove. A proposed rule goes through four questions,
in order:

1. **Can the syntax of one file decide it?** Then it belongs in a linter such as Ruff.
2. **Is it a type error, or can an annotation express it?** Then it belongs in a type checker
   such as ty.
3. **Is it about which modules may import which?** Then it belongs in tach or import-linter.
4. **Does it need at least one of the proofs below?** Only then is it a heki rule.

A heki rule is measured on a corpus and reviewed by hand before it is enabled by default. Where
another tool covers part of it, heki keeps only the rest (`EFF107` and Ruff's `RUF006`).

The proofs heki can make, on five axes:

| Axis | What heki establishes | Used by |
| ---- | --------------------- | ------- |
| Control flow | which statements can run after which: CFG paths, loops and their bounds, exception edges | `MUT106`, `MUT109`, `MUT113`, `EFF102`, `EFF103`, `EFF106`, `EFF109`, `EFF110`, `DATA101`, `OPT` |
| Calls | which functions a call reaches across modules, and what they do (summaries propagated over the call graph) | `EFF101`, `EFF109`, `EFF110`, `EFF201`, `MUT103`, `MUT108`, `MUT109`, `MUT110`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`, `MUT201`–`MUT204` |
| Aliases | which names, iterators, and views refer to one object; whether it is unique to its frame and of an exact builtin type | `MUT202`, `MUT201`, `MUT204`, `MUT108`, `MUT110`, `MUT112`, `EFF107`, `EFF109`, `EFF110`, `OPT101`–`OPT130` |
| Effects | which blocking, network, file, or database work runs, from the catalog of library behavior | `EFF101`–`EFF106`, `EFF201`, `DATA101` |
| State | which attributes and containers a function reads, writes, or mutates, and who may do so | `MUT101`, `MUT107`, `MUT108`, `MUT109`, `MUT110`, `MUT111`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`, `MUT201`–`MUT204` |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/installation/

# Installation

heki is a single executable: its Python package ships only that executable and installs no
Python dependencies into your environment.

## With uv, pipx, or pip

=== "uv"

    ```console
    $ uv tool install heki
    $ uvx heki check            # or run it without installing
    ```

=== "pipx"

    ```console
    $ pipx install heki
    ```

=== "pip"

    ```console
    $ pip install heki
    ```

As a development dependency of a project:

```console
$ uv add --dev heki
```

Wheels are published for these platforms:

| OS | Architectures |
| -- | ------------- |
| Linux | x86-64, AArch64, x86-64 musl |
| macOS | Apple silicon, Intel |
| Windows | x86-64 |

## From source

heki needs Rust 1.99 or newer:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki
$ cd heki
$ cargo install --path crates/heki
```

## Check the installation

```console
$ heki --version
$ heki rule --all
```

## Supported Python versions

- heki analyzes code written for Python 3.11 to 3.15.
- It does not need a Python interpreter to run.
- The version of the checked code comes from
  [`target-version`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings), or from `requires-python`; see
  [Scope](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#the-target-python-version) for what it changes.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/

# Getting Started

This page runs heki on a project, reads a diagnostic, applies a fix, and picks the rules.

## Run it

From the root of a project (the directory with `pyproject.toml`):

```console
$ heki check
$ heki check --heuristic
```

The first command runs the exact rules and the rules of the [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts)
you declare. An exact rule is certified: every report it made on the development corpus and on a
frozen holdout corpus was checked by hand, and none was false
([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications)). In 0.2.0 the exact rules are `EFF101`,
`EFF103`, `DATA101`, `MUT110`, `MUT114`, the proven tier of the `OPT` rewrite rules (the reports
whose rewrite heki proves safe), and the exact tier of `OPT113`. A text run says how many
heuristic rules it left off. `--heuristic` runs those too; their reports can be wrong about the
code, and every output labels them.

heki checks every Python file under the current directory, except the
[excluded and ignored ones](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#which-files-are-checked). Pass files or directories
to narrow it:

```console
$ heki check src/ tests/test_api.py
```

## Read a diagnostic

```console
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 (async-blocking-call) [warning] `app.users.load_user` always runs the waiting call `requests.get` on the event loop (1 call down, on every path)
  |
5 |     user = load_user(user_id)
  |            ^
  = related: app/api.py:5:12: `handler` calls `app.users.load_user`
  = related: app/users.py:5:12: `load_user` calls `requests.get`
  = help: offload it with `asyncio.to_thread`, or use an async client
```

| Part | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `app/api.py:5:12` | where to look |
| `EFF101 (async-blocking-call)` | the rule's code and name |
| `[warning]` | its severity: `error` for a bug (a wrong result, an exception, a lost update, a deadlock, a broken contract), `warning` for slower code, as here, or for a bug that is rarely harmful. An error makes `heki check` fail; a warning is shown without failing it, unless `--fail-on warning` (`lint.fail-on = "warning"`) is set. A heuristic report adds `heuristic` (`[warning, heuristic]`): it can be wrong about the code, as a premise of its claim can be open |
| the message | what heki established, in one sentence: here, that the call to `load_user` always runs `requests.get`, a call that waits on the network, on the event loop |
| `related` lines | the hops of the chain of calls behind it, to follow it across files; editors show them as related information you can jump to |
| `help` line | what to do about it |

`heki rule EFF101` explains the rule, its exclusions, and what to do instead. The
[rules reference](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) has the same text for every rule.

## Fix what heki can prove

`--fix` applies the rewrites heki proves safe and always faster (`OPT101`, `OPT102`), and
`--diff` shows them first:

```console
$ heki check --diff
--- a/app/report.py
+++ b/app/report.py
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 def rows_of(items):
     rows = []
     for item in items:
-        rows = rows + [item]
+        rows.append(item)
     return rows
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
$ heki check --fix
Fixed 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

`--fix` then reports what is left, such as the `EFF101` above, which has no automatic fix.

When heki cannot prove a fix safe, the help says why, nothing is rewritten, and the report is
heuristic whatever the rule's certainty. Here the list is also handed to other code inside the
loop:

```console
$ heki check --heuristic app/shared.py
app/shared.py:4:9: OPT101 (list-quadratic-concat) [warning, heuristic] `rows = rows + [...]` copies the whole list each time it runs in the loop
  |
4 |         rows = rows + [item]
  |         ^
  = help: append in place with `rows.append(...)` / `rows.extend(...)` [not auto-fixable: Unique(rows): it may be shared: passed to code heki cannot see (line 5)]

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 1 file(s).
```

[Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/) lists which rules are fixed, and what a fix must prove.

## Silence a diagnostic

Append a suppression comment to the reported line:

```python
user = load_user(user_id)  # heki: ignore[EFF101]
```

The other forms (`# heki: ignore`, `# noqa: EFF101`) and `per-file-ignores` are in
[Inline suppressions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#inline-suppressions).

## Choose the rules

```console
$ heki check --select EFF,MUT        # only these families
$ heki check --extend-select EFF105  # add an opt-in rule
$ heki check --ignore OPT110         # everything except one rule
```

Codes, code prefixes, and rule names (`async-blocking-call`) are accepted. A prefix does not
enable the opt-in rules, nor the heuristic ones without `--heuristic`: see
[Rule selection](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint).

## Output formats

```console
$ heki check --output-format json
```

| Format | Prints |
| ------ | ------ |
| `full` (default) | each diagnostic with its source line, call chain, and help |
| `concise` | one line per diagnostic: the message, without the help |
| `json` | every field: also the help, the evidence, the blocker that stops a fix, and the fix edits ([fields](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#after-an-edit-heki-check)) |
| `github` | GitHub Actions annotations with the message ([CI](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#continuous-integration)) |
| `sarif` | the message, the location, the call chain, and the help (`properties.help`), for code-scanning dashboards (no evidence or blocker) |

Every format, `--diff`, and the errors of files that cannot be read or parsed print a file's
path relative to the working directory when the file is inside it (otherwise as given), as Ruff
does, and with `/` separators on every platform, Windows included.

### Colors

On a terminal, the `full` and `concise` output and `--diff` are colored as Ruff colors its
output: paths in bold, rule codes in red, the severity, the source frame and its caret, and the
lines a diff removes and adds. The same variables and option as Ruff's decide it, each row over
the rows above it:

| Setting | Colors |
| ------- | ------ |
| stdout is a terminal / a pipe or a file | on / off |
| `NO_COLOR` set (to anything), or `CLICOLOR=0` | off |
| `FORCE_COLOR` set to anything but the empty string, or `CLICOLOR_FORCE` to anything but `0` | on (for a CI log that shows colors) |
| `--color always` / `--color never` | on / off |

`json`, `github`, and `sarif` output never holds colors, and the summary and the errors heki
writes to stderr are not colored.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `0` | no diagnostics, or only warnings (they are printed) |
| `1` | an error found, or a warning with `--fail-on warning` (`lint.fail-on = "warning"`), among the Ratchet regressions when a baseline is used; also when `--update-baseline` refuses a grown entry, or `--diff` would change files |
| `2` | configuration error, unreadable file, unknown rule, or syntax error |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/

# Configuration

heki reads `[tool.heki]` from `pyproject.toml`, or a `heki.toml` / `.heki.toml` file with the same
keys without the `tool.heki` prefix. Keys are kebab-case, as in Ruff.

```toml
[tool.heki]
target-version = "py312"            # default: inferred from project.requires-python
extend-exclude = ["generated"]      # added to the default excludes
baseline = "heki-baseline.toml"     # Ratchet baseline (heki check, --watch, the server)

[tool.heki.lint]
select = ["MUT", "EFF", "DATA", "OPT"]
extend-select = ["EFF105"]
ignore = ["OPT110"]
per-file-ignores = { "tests/**" = ["EFF"], "scripts/*.py" = ["OPT"] }
relax-async-in-tests = true
fail-on = "warning"                 # warnings fail heki check too (default: "error")

[tool.heki.lint.severity]
OPT103 = "warning"
```

## Where heki finds the configuration

1. The project root is the nearest directory at or above the first path given (the current
   directory when no path is given) that holds `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, or `pyproject.toml`.
   The search stops at the top of the enclosing Git working tree (the directory holding `.git`):
   a configuration above it belongs to another project. Without a configuration file, the root
   is the current directory, as Ruff and ty take it, when it holds the first path; but never a
   directory above the top of the Git working tree (then the root is that top), and outside the
   current directory and any Git working tree it is the first path's own directory (the
   directory given, or the given file's directory). The language server takes its workspace
   folder for the current directory.
2. heki reads the first of `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, and `pyproject.toml` in that directory. A
   `pyproject.toml` without `[tool.heki]` still marks the root: its project gets the defaults.
3. `--config <path>` names the file instead. The project root stays where step 1 finds it.

One run checks one project: its configuration applies to every file of the run, also to files
given from another project. `heki check a/one.py b/two.py` uses `a/`'s configuration for both, so
check projects with their own configurations in separate runs: `heki check a/`, then
`heki check b/`.

### Which tables hold the settings

The file's name decides, as Ruff reads `pyproject.toml` and `ruff.toml`:

- A file named `pyproject.toml` holds the settings in `[tool.heki]` (`[tool.heki.lint]`,
  `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`, ...). Its other tables belong to the packaging standards and other
  tools, and heki does not read them.
- Any other file (`heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, or the file `--config` names, whatever its name)
  holds the same keys at its top level, without the `tool.heki` prefix (`[lint]`,
  `[[ecosystem]]`).

heki never ignores a setting. These are configuration errors (exit code 2):

- an unknown key in any of heki's tables (the message names it: ``unknown field `bogus` ``);
- a `[tool.heki]` table in a file that is not named `pyproject.toml`;
- a heki setting at the top level of a `pyproject.toml` (`[[ecosystem]]` instead of
  `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`).

### Module names follow the source roots

Module names are the paths below a source root (`app/api.py` is `app.api` below the project
root, `src/acme/io.py` is `acme.io` below `src`). heki resolves the imports between the
project's modules by these names, and they appear in messages that name a function by its full
name and in the `target`s of [baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) entries, whose `path`s
are relative to the project root.

- The `src` setting lists the source roots: directories relative to the project root, like
  Ruff's `src` and ty's `environment.root`. A file below several of them is named below the
  deepest one, and a file below none is named below the project root. `src` does not accept
  globs yet (Ruff's does): list the directories.
- Without `src`, heki detects the source roots as ty does: `src`, the directory named after the
  project (`project.name` of the `pyproject.toml`, else the root's own name) when it holds a
  directory of the same name (`acme/acme/`), and `python` (the maturin layout), each when it is
  a directory and not a package (no `__init__.py`). A source root that is a package is imported
  by its own name (`src.helpers`).
- Other layouts need `src`: a subdirectory application whose directories are imported as
  top-level packages (`backend/config/env.py` imported as `config.env`) takes
  `src = ["backend"]`, and a `lib/` layout (`lib/matplotlib`) takes `src = ["lib"]`.

Without a configuration file the project root is where heki runs (see above): in a repository
without one, `heki check` run in `services/api/` names `services/api/app.py` `app`, and its
`from helpers import slow` finds `services/api/helpers.py`; run from the top of the repository,
the same file is `services.api.app` and the import is not resolved. Put a `pyproject.toml` or a
`heki.toml` in the project's directory to fix the root wherever heki runs.

## Top-level settings

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `target-version` | the oldest version `project.requires-python` admits, else `py312` | Python version of the code: `py311` … `py315` (or `3.11` … `3.15`). `--target-version` overrides it. See [below](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#the-default-target-version) for the inference and [Scope](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#the-target-python-version) for what the version changes. |
| `exclude` | the Ruff defaults (`.git`, `.venv`, `build`, `dist`, `node_modules`, …) | Replaces the excluded paths: globs, matched against the project-relative path and each of its components, and covering everything below a matched directory. |
| `extend-exclude` | `[]` | Adds excluded paths. |
| `src` | the detected source roots | Source roots, relative to the project root: the module names of the files below each are relative to it (`src = ["lib"]` names `lib/pkg/net.py` `pkg.net`). See [Module names follow the source roots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#module-names-follow-the-source-roots). |
| `baseline` | none | Ratchet baseline file, relative to the project root, used when `--baseline` is not given: by `heki check`, `--watch`, and the language server. See [Ratchet baselines](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines). |

### The default target version

Without `target-version`, heki reads `requires-python` from the `pyproject.toml` that holds the
configuration, or from the one next to `heki.toml` or the `--config` file. It takes the oldest
supported version that every clause admits:

| `requires-python` | Target |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| `>=3.11` | `py311` |
| `>=3.11, !=3.11.*` | `py312` |
| `>=3.9, <3.11` (only older versions) | `py311` |
| `>=3.16` (only newer versions) | `py315` |
| `<4` (no lower bound, admits 3.12) | `py312` |
| missing, or not a version specifier | `py312` |

### Which files are checked

- Without paths, `heki check` checks every `.py` and `.pyi` file under the current directory.
- Discovery skips hidden files and directories, the paths `exclude` and `extend-exclude` match,
  and the entries of `.gitignore` (inside a Git repository), `.ignore`, and `.hekiignore` files.
- Files named on the command line are always checked.

## Rule selection: `[tool.heki.lint]`

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `select` | the exact rules and the contract rules | Rules to enable instead of the defaults. An empty list enables no rule before `extend-select`, as in Ruff. |
| `extend-select` | `[]` | Rules to add. |
| `ignore` | `[]` | Rules to disable. |
| `per-file-ignores` | `{}` | Glob → rules disabled in matching files (project-relative POSIX paths). As in Ruff, `*` also matches `/`: `scripts/*.py` covers `scripts/tools/worker.py` too. |
| `severity` | `"warning"` for the rules that report slower code (`EFF101`, `EFF102`, `EFF103`, `EFF105`, `EFF111`, `EFF113`, `DATA101`, and the `OPT` rules) and for `MUT110`, which reports a bug that is rarely harmful; `"error"` for the others, which report bugs | Rule → `"error"` or `"warning"`. It changes the output and the SARIF level. By default only errors make `heki check` fail; `fail-on = "warning"` makes warnings fail it too. |
| `relax-async-in-tests` | `true` | Skip `EFF101`, `EFF111`, `EFF105`, and `EFF106` in test code as pytest finds it: `test_*` functions and the functions nested in them, `test_*.py` and `*_test.py` files, and files under `test/` or `tests/`. |
| `heuristic` | `false` | Whether the heuristic rules that are not opt-in run by default and for a prefix or `ALL`, as the exact rules do. `--heuristic` and `--no-heuristic` override it. |
| `fail-on` | `"error"` | The least severity whose reports make `heki check` (and `--watch`) exit with code 1: `"error"`, or `"warning"` to fail on warnings too. Warnings are reported either way, and the language server shows them. `--fail-on` overrides it. |

- A rule is named by its code (`EFF101`), its name (`async-blocking-call`), a code prefix
  (`EFF`, `MUT2`), or `ALL`. An unknown rule is a configuration error.
- Every rule is exact or heuristic ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)). The defaults, a prefix, and
  `ALL` enable the exact rules and the contract rules; with `heuristic = true` they also enable
  the heuristic rules that are not opt-in, as Ruff's `preview` does. Its code or name enables a
  heuristic rule either way.
- An exact rule's report that did not establish every premise of its claim (an `OPT` report
  whose rewrite is not proven) is heuristic, and is shown where a heuristic rule would run: with
  `heuristic = true`, or when its code or name is selected.
- A run of `full` or `concise` output that leaves heuristic rules off, or heuristic reports out,
  says how many.
- A prefix or `ALL` never enables the opt-in rules (`EFF105`, `EFF106`, `EFF107`, `EFF109`,
  `EFF110`, `MUT101`, `MUT103`, `MUT106`, `MUT107`, `MUT108`, `MUT111`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`,
  `MUT115`): they
  need their exact code or name. In `ignore`, a prefix covers every rule it matches.
- The command line wins: `--select` replaces `select`, `--extend-select` and `--ignore` add to the
  configured lists, and `--heuristic` / `--no-heuristic` replace `heuristic`.

```toml
[tool.heki.lint]
heuristic = true   # also the heuristic rules that are not opt-in
```

## Contracts

Contracts declare what no type can say. Each kind is an array of tables with its own rule:

| Contract | Declares | Rule | Certainty |
| -------- | -------- | ---- | --------- |
| [`write-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#write-owners) | who may write an attribute | `MUT201`; `MUT205` with `unresolved = "report"` | heuristic |
| [`read-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#read-owners) | who may read an attribute | `MUT203`; `MUT206` with `unresolved = "report"` | heuristic |
| [`call-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#call-owners) | who may call a function or construct a class | `MUT204`; `MUT207` with `unresolved = "report"` | heuristic |
| [`effect-boundaries`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#effect-boundaries) | what a scope must not reach: I/O, writes, reads, or calls | `EFF201` | heuristic |
| [`readonly-returns`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#readonly-returns) | results every caller shares | `MUT202` | heuristic |
| [`invalidation`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#invalidation) | writes that must be announced | `MUT109` | heuristic |

- These rules report nothing until a contract exists. The results of `functools.lru_cache` /
  `functools.cache` functions are checked without one by `MUT114` (`cached-result-mutation`).
- Declaring a contract selects its rule, whatever its certainty.
- Every name in a contract is a dotted pattern. It matches the full name or any dotted suffix
  (`DataModel.fields` matches `pkg.model.DataModel.fields`, not `pkg.BigModel.fields`), and it
  may be a glob (`*`, `?`, `[...]`, `{a,b}`).
- A glob's `*` spans dots (`pkg.parser.*` covers the functions of every module under
  `pkg.parser`), except in the last segment of a target, which names the attribute, function,
  method, or class: `pkg.*._*` names the private members of everything in `pkg`, and no function
  of a private module whose own name is public; `pkg.api_*` names `pkg.api_commit`, not
  `pkg.api_helpers.api_reset`.
- A name with a module part, `module:qualname`, names definitions of the project modules the
  part names, never of their submodules. The module part matches the whole module name, exactly
  or as a glob (`pkg.*:run`), not a suffix; the qualified name after the colon matches the whole
  name inside the module, a `*` spanning dots. `pkg:*` names everything `pkg/__init__.py`
  defines (its functions, classes, methods, nested functions, and module body `<module>`), where
  `pkg.*` also covers `pkg.sub.user.sub_user`; `pkg.sub:Store.*` names the methods of `Store` in
  `pkg.sub`. In a `Class.attr` target the module part belongs to the class
  (`pkg.model:DataModel.fields`), and a call target with one is matched whole (`pkg:*` names
  every function, method, and class of `pkg`). Such a name never matches an external symbol, and
  `unresolved = "report"` counts its last name (`decide` of `pkg:decide`). A module part that
  names no project module is no error: the name matches nothing.
- A report of a glob target names the member it matched (`reads
  `pkg.types.DataType._flag``); one report standing for several members lists the others.
- An access matching several targets of one contract (a target on a class and one on its
  subclass, a protocol's member and its implementation's attribute) is one report of the
  contract: it names the target configured first among them, and lists the others (`(also
  `A.items`)`).
- A `Class.attr` target covers the subclasses of the class too.
- A contract heki cannot use is a configuration error: a target that is not `Class.attr`, an
  invalid glob, a name with more than one colon or an empty module or qualified name, call
  targets whose globs are too many to match together (tens of thousands of complex ones), an
  argument list heki cannot read, an invalid glob in `allowed-protocols`, or an unknown value of
  `forbid`, `fresh-objects`, `unresolved`, `references`, `attribution`, `own-receiver`, or
  `unlisted-dict-keys`.
- With `unresolved = "report"`, a contract also reports the accesses it cannot tie to a class,
  each under its own rule (`MUT205` writes, `MUT206` reads, `MUT207` calls): an attribute or
  method named like a target, accessed on an object of unknown class (an unannotated parameter,
  a loop variable, an untyped call result, `Any`, a protocol whose implementations heki cannot
  list). A baseline counts them apart from the violations the typed rules prove.
- An attribute named through a string (`setattr`, `getattr`, `__dict__`, `vars`) is followed
  when the string is a constant: see [Dynamic names](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#dynamic-names).

### `write-owners`

```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "generation-store"
targets = ["pkg.model.DataModel.fields", "DataType.data_types", 'DataModelFieldBase.extras["init"]']
allowed-writers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*", "Store.*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__", "copy_deep"]
forbid-cached-property-on = ["DataModel"]
message = "use GenerationStore.set_fields() instead"
fresh-objects = "allow"
unresolved = "report"
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` attributes, or `Class.attr["key"]` for one entry of the container an attribute holds. |
| `allowed-writers` | `[]` | Functions allowed to write the targets. |
| `forbidden-writers` | `[]` | When set, only writes by these functions are reported: see [Allowed and forbidden functions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#allowed-and-forbidden-functions). |
| `exempt-methods` | `[]` | Construction and copy methods allowed to write the targets. A plain name (`__deepcopy__`) matches any method of that name; a name with a dot or a glob (`DataModel.copy_deep`, `create_*`) is a pattern, as in `allowed-writers`. |
| `forbid-cached-property-on` | `[]` | Classes on which defining a `@cached_property` is itself reported. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract: where to write instead. |
| `fresh-objects` | `"allow"` | `"allow"` or `"report"`: whether a write that constructs the object it writes is reported. |
| `unresolved` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether the writes the contract cannot tie to a class are reported under [`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/). |
| `attribution` | `"call-graph"` | `"call-graph"` or `"lexical"`: which function a write is judged in. See [How contracts report](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#how-contracts-report). |
| `own-receiver` | `"report"` | `"report"` or `"allow"`: whether a write through the receiver of the method it is judged in (`self`, `cls`, `super()`) is allowed. See [How contracts report](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#how-contracts-report). |
| `allowed-protocols` | `[]` | Project protocols (class patterns, their subclasses included): a write through a value typed with one that declares the attribute, itself or through its protocol bases, is allowed. See [How contracts report](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#how-contracts-report). |
| `unlisted-dict-keys` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether a `__dict__` key of a target's class that no target names is reported when it is written. |

A container entry (`Class.attr["key"]`):

- matches the writes of that constant key (a literal or a string constant), not a write of the
  whole container or with a computed key;
- is reported once, under the entry, when its container is a target too.

A write into the entries of a target's container (`model.meta["kw"][name] = v`) is a write of
the target.

With `fresh-objects = "allow"`, a write is no violation when it constructs the object it writes:

- the object was allocated in the same call chain: by calling its class, by `object.__new__`
  (`object.__new__(Node)`), by a copy, or by a project function returning a new object;
- nothing can hold it yet: no store, `yield`, closure, or call that may keep it ran before the
  write.

A shallow copy's containers are the original's: only rebinding its attributes constructs it.

With `unlisted-dict-keys = "report"`, `MUT201` also reports a constant key written through the
namespace of an object of a class a target covers (`field.__dict__[KEY] = v`,
`field.__dict__.setdefault("_cache", v)`, `del vars(field)["k"]`) when no target covering that
class names the key, so a new cache key needs a target first. A target names the keys its
attribute pattern matches (`Field._*` names `_cache`), and an entry target names its container.
The contract's allowance applies as to a target write. A key computed at run time has no name to
check (`MUT205`, with `unresolved = "report"`), and neither has a write in a helper that does not
type the object.

With `unresolved = "report"`, `MUT205` reports:

- an attribute named like a target, written on an object of unknown class;
- a computed attribute name (`setattr(obj, name, v)`, `obj.__dict__[name] = v`,
  `obj.__dict__.update(...)`, `vars(obj) |= other`) written on a target class, or on an object
  of unknown class, where it may be any target.

### `read-owners`

```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["pkg.reference.Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*", "*GenerationStore*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__"]
message = "read children through GenerationIndex instead"
unresolved = "report"
```

The read side of `write-owners`. A read is `ref.children`, a read through a local alias,
`getattr(ref, "children")`, or `ref.__dict__["children"]`, also through a class object, which
reads the class attribute (`Reference.children`, `cls.children`, a value typed
`type[Reference]`).

A read, or a call (`call-owners`, and an effect boundary's `call-targets` and
`allowed-callees`), through a value typed with a project protocol that declares the member is
judged by the protocol, the type the code uses it through: `def f(h: Host): h._m` reads
`Host._m`, not `_m` of the classes implementing `Host`, and a private method of an
implementation called through the protocol keeps what it reads and calls. A write through such
a value still writes the implementations' attribute. `allowed-protocols` allows the reads, calls,
and writes through the protocols it names (see [How contracts report](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#how-contracts-report)).

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` attributes. A container entry (`Class.attr["key"]`) is a write target only, and a configuration error here. |
| `allowed-readers` | `[]` | Functions allowed to read the targets. |
| `forbidden-readers` | `[]` | When set, only reads by these functions are reported. |
| `exempt-methods` | `[]` | Methods allowed to read the targets, matched as in `write-owners`. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract. |
| `unresolved` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether the reads of a target's attribute name on an object of unknown class are reported under [`MUT206`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/). |
| `attribution` | `"call-graph"` | `"call-graph"` or `"lexical"`, as in `write-owners`. |
| `own-receiver` | `"report"` | `"report"` or `"allow"`, as in `write-owners`. |
| `allowed-protocols` | `[]` | As in `write-owners`, for a read or a call through the protocol. |

`MUT203` does not see a read through a parameter without a project-class annotation; with
`unresolved = "report"`, `MUT206` reports it unless every caller binds the parameter to an
instance of a project class outside the targets' classes.

### `call-owners`

```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference", "pkg.util.reset_cache", "FinalFacts"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*"]
exempt-methods = ["__deepcopy__"]
message = "use a GenerationStore operation instead"
unresolved = "report"
```

The call side of `write-owners`.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | Functions, methods, or classes. A `Class.method` target covers the method's overrides in subclasses; a class target means constructing the class or a subclass. A target may end in an argument list (`DataType(is_dict=True)`, below). |
| `subclasses` | `true` | `false`: a class target means constructing exactly the class, not a subclass (an exception class whose subclasses anyone may raise). `Class.method` targets keep covering overrides. |
| `allowed-callers` | `[]` | Functions allowed to call the targets. |
| `forbidden-callers` | `[]` | When set, only calls by these functions are reported. |
| `exempt-methods` | `[]` | Methods allowed to call the targets, matched as in `write-owners`. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract. |
| `unresolved` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"` or `"report"`: whether the calls of a method named like a target (its last name) on an object of unknown class are reported under [`MUT207`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/). |
| `references` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"`, `"calls"`, `"calls-and-bases"`, or `"reads"`: whether a reference handing a target on to be called later counts as a call of it (`[decide]`, `return decide`, `partial(decide)`, `field(default_factory=Rule)`, `obj.callback = self.decide`), with `"calls-and-bases"` a class statement naming a class target among its bases too (`class Derived(Base)`), and with `"reads"` every other use of a target's value as well (`Keys.of(...)`, `Code.OK`, `isinstance(x, Keys)`, `case Keys():`, `tuple[Keys, int]`). |
| `attribution` | `"call-graph"` | `"call-graph"` or `"lexical"`, as in `write-owners`. |
| `own-receiver` | `"report"` | `"report"` or `"allow"`, as in `write-owners`. |
| `allowed-protocols` | `[]` | As in `write-owners`, for a read or a call through the protocol. |

- A call is reported only when every function it may call (each candidate in the class
  hierarchy) is a target: `text.replace(...)` on a `str` is never a call of
  `DataType.replace_reference`.
- Bound-method aliases (`replace = dt.replace_reference`) and `getattr(dt, "replace_reference")`
  with a constant name are followed.
- The targets of a contract may call each other: a call of the guarded operation is checked where
  it is made, so what the operation does inside is part of it.
- With `references = "calls"`, a target handed on is reported where it is named ("`f` hands on
  `pkg.core.decide`"; a name an import or the module body binds, read in the scope binding it, at
  the statement handing it on; a name a class body, a function, a lambda, or a comprehension
  nested in a function reads from it, a local import included, at the name): passed to a call, stored in an attribute, an item, or a global, returned,
  yielded, raised, or held by a display that is. A use that only names it is no reference: an
  argument of `isinstance`, `issubclass`, another builtin that only inspects its arguments
  (`print`, `getattr`, `type`), `super`, `typing.cast`, `typing.TypeVar`, `typing.NewType`, or
  `contextlib.suppress`; an `except` clause, a class's bases and keywords, a default or an
  annotation of a function; a subscript (`Optional[Rule]`), a comparison, a receiver
  (`Rule.of(...)`), and a module binding another name to it (an import, `run = core.decide`). A
  callable a builtin calls once per item (`sorted(xs, key=decide)`) is a call already.
- A target ending in an argument list, `name(parameter=value, ...)`, names the calls of `name`
  that pass each value: `"DataType(is_dict=True)"`, `'container_flags(kind="dict")'`. A value is
  `True`, `False`, `None`, an integer, or a string in single or double quotes (no escapes). A call
  passes it when heki establishes that the argument bound to the parameter is that constant (a
  literal, a string constant bound once, such as a module's `Final` name, or a module's number or
  boolean bound once, as `EFF101` evaluates them: `LIMIT = 0`, also imported (by the module or by
  a function) or read as an attribute of its module (`settings.LIMIT`), unless a module rebinds
  it; an imported name the importing module binds again in a function declaring it
  `global`, in another module-level store, or with `del`, or that a star import may rebind, is no
  constant there): passed by keyword (also to a class without a project `__init__`, a dataclass or a
  pydantic model), by position where every function the call may run binds that position to the
  parameter, or left out where every such function's default is the value and only `True`,
  `False`, `None`, `0`, or `""` (heki keeps defaults by class and truthiness). A keyword binds as
  Python binds it: never a positional-only parameter (with `def f(kind=False, /, **kwargs)`,
  `f(kind=True)` leaves `kind` false), and a keyword naming no parameter passes its value under its
  name into `**kwargs`; the receiver of a method call is its first position. A `**` operand that is
  a dict display with string constant keys (literals, or string constants as above), which nothing
  changes (a name holding it is only unpacked with `**`, bound to another name, tested, or
  returned), passes its entries as keywords: `DataType(**{"is_dict": True})`,
  `flags = {"is_dict": True}; DataType(**flags)`. A call that raises `TypeError` instead of running
  the function passes nothing: two keywords of one name (written and in such a display, or in two
  displays), a keyword binding a parameter a position or the receiver binds too, a keyword naming no
  parameter of a function without `**kwargs`, a position (the receiver included) past the parameters
  of a function without `*args`, or a parameter without a default left unbound where no `*`
  unpacking or `**` unpacking of another mapping may bind it. Any other argument (a variable, a
  call, `*` unpacking, `**` unpacking of another mapping) is not established, and the call is not
  reported. A reference passes no arguments, so it never matches. A target with an argument list
  names no symbol outside the project; `unresolved = "report"` matches its last name before the
  list, whatever the arguments of a call on an object of unknown class.
- With `references = "calls-and-bases"`, a class statement passing a class target as a base is
  reported too ("`<module>` subclasses `pkg.core.Base`"), at the base, or at the class statement
  for a name an import or the module body binds: the class it makes holds the base, and
  constructing it runs the base's initialization unless it overrides it. A base is the value the
  statement passes, typed where the statement runs as any value is (a parameter, a local, or a
  class-body name of the imported class's name is another value), and matched as a construction
  is (with `subclasses = false`, the class itself only); a keyword (`metaclass=Base`) is no base.
- With `references = "reads"`, everything `"calls-and-bases"` counts is reported as before, and
  every other use of a target's value is reported too ("`f` reads `pkg.core.Keys`"), where it is
  named as a hand-on is: the object of an attribute read, store, or deletion and a method's
  receiver (`Keys.of(names)`, `Keys.__annotations__`, `Code.OK`), an argument of a call that only
  names it (`isinstance(value, Keys)`, `cast(Keys, x)`, `TypeVar("T", bound=Keys)`), a subscript
  or its index (`tuple[Keys, int]`, `Optional[Keys]`), an operand (`f is decide`, `Keys | None`),
  a tested condition (`if decide:`), an iterated, awaited, formatted, or `with` value, a dict
  display's key, the class of a class pattern (`case Keys():`), the types of an `except` clause
  an exception may reach, a decorator, a default of a function or lambda, a keyword of a class
  statement, and the cause of `raise ... from`, also through copies and the displays holding it
  (`isinstance(value, (Keys, Code))`, a test of a module-level display holding it). No read: a
  call (a call of its own), an annotation, evaluated or not (`list[Keys]`, `Keys | None`), the
  values Python evaluates only when asked (a `type` statement's value, the bounds and defaults of
  type parameters), an import, a name bound to the target by itself (`Alias = Keys`, a local, a
  `nonlocal` cell), whose own uses count, and a value nothing uses (`Keys` as an expression
  statement). A load handing a target on is reported as a hand-on only. A read is matched as a
  construction is, so a subclass counts unless `subclasses = false`; an instance of the class is
  no read of it.

### Allowed and forbidden functions

`allowed-writers`, `allowed-readers`, and `allowed-callers` name the functions a contract
allows. `forbidden-writers`, `forbidden-readers`, and `forbidden-callers` name where it applies
instead, so a layer rule ("the parser must not read `Reference.children`") needs no list of every
other layer:

```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "parser-reads"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
forbidden-readers = ["pkg.parser.*"]
allowed-readers = ["pkg.parser.index.*"]
```

| `allowed-*` | `forbidden-*` | Reported |
| ----------- | ------------- | -------- |
| unset | unset | every access |
| set | unset | accesses outside the allowed functions |
| unset | set | accesses by the forbidden functions |
| set | set | accesses by the forbidden functions, except the allowed ones |

- An access counts as one by a forbidden function when the function that is reported, a private
  helper it hands the access through, or the function making the access is forbidden (with
  `attribution = "lexical"`, the function holding the access).
- `allowed-*` and `exempt-methods` win wherever they apply on that path, as does the rule for
  functions that [only run inside allowed functions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#how-contracts-report).

### `effect-boundaries`

```toml
[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "pure-render"
scopes = ["*.render", "*.render_module_code", "pkg.domain.*"]
forbid = ["writes-targets", "blocking"]
write-targets = ["DataModel.*", "DataType.*"]
allowed-callees = ["pkg.logging.*"]
message = "render entry points must not mutate model state"

[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "decisions-read-final-facts"
scopes = ["pkg.model._decisions.*"]
forbid = ["reads-targets", "calls"]
read-targets = ["DataType.is_optional", "DataModel._additional_imports"]
call-targets = ["GenerationStore.*"]

[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "pass-sort-base-classes"
scopes = ["pkg.parser.passes.sort_base_classes"]
allow-writes = ["DataModel.base_classes"]
write-universe = ["DataModel.*", "DataModelFieldBase.*", "DataType.*"]

[[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
name = "portable-generation"
scopes = ["pkg.generate.*"]
forbid = ["reads-environment"]
import-probes = "report"
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The boundary's name in reports. |
| `scopes` | `[]` | Modules, classes, or functions whose functions must stay inside the boundary; nested functions are included. A module body is included only where a pattern names `<module>` (`pkg.gen:<module>`, below). |
| `forbid` | `[]` | What the scope functions must not reach (tokens below). |
| `write-targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` targets of `writes-targets`, required with it. `Class.attr["key"]` names one entry, as in `write-owners`. |
| `read-targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` targets of `reads-targets`, required with it: reads as `read-owners` sees them, also inside property getters. A container entry is a configuration error. An entry can also name an attribute of a module outside the project by its full name (`sys.platform`, `os.environ`, below). |
