| `call-targets` | `[]` | Functions, methods, or classes of `calls`, required with it, matched as the `targets` of `call-owners` (also with an argument list). An entry can also name a function or class outside the project by its full name (`os.getenv`, `platform.*`, below). |
| `write-universe` | `[]` | `Class.attr` entries: a reached write of one that `allow-writes` does not name is reported, once per written `Class.attr`. |
| `allow-writes` | `[]` | `Class.attr` writes the boundary allows, exempt from `write-targets` too. Needs `write-universe`. |
| `allowed-callees` | `[]` | Functions, classes, modules, or ecosystem symbols whose effects are allowed: paths through them are not followed, and calls of them are no `calls` violation. |
| `fresh-objects` | `"allow"` | `"allow"` or `"report"`: whether a write that constructs the object it writes (as in `write-owners`) counts as a write of the boundary. |
| `references` | `"ignore"` | `"ignore"`, `"calls"`, `"calls-and-bases"`, or `"reads"`, as for `call-owners`: whether a reference handing a `call-targets` entry on (and a class statement naming one among its bases, and any other use of its value) counts for `calls`. |
| `import-probes` | `"allow"` | `"allow"` or `"report"`: whether `reads-environment` also forbids an import probe, an `import` inside a `try` with an `except` clause naming `ImportError` or `ModuleNotFoundError`. `"report"` without `reads-environment` is a configuration error. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the boundary. |

| `forbid` token | Forbids |
| -------------- | ------- |
| `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `blocking-fs`, `blocking-subprocess`, `blocking-sync`, `sleep` | that blocking effect |
| `blocking` | all six blocking effects |
| `mutates-params` | changing a parameter in place (for a method, `self` is a parameter) |
| `writes-targets` | writing a `write-targets` attribute |
| `reads-targets` | reading a `read-targets` attribute |
| `calls` | calling a `call-targets` function or class |
| `reads-environment` | reading the environment the program runs in: calling or reading what the ecosystem catalog tags `environment` (below), and import probes with `import-probes = "report"` |

Outside the project, `call-targets` and `read-targets` entries name symbols by their full dotted
name, starting with the top-level module: `os.getenv` matches a call of `os.getenv` (also
`from os import getenv`, `import os as o`), `platform.*` every function of `platform`, and
`sys.platform` a read of `sys.platform` (also `from sys import platform`, or `import sys as s`
and `s.platform`). A dotted suffix (`getenv`), a leading glob (`*.getenv`), or a module part (`os:getenv`) never
names a symbol outside the project, so an entry for project functions keeps its meaning. Only a call or a read
heki resolves counts: an attribute read by name (`getattr(sys, name)`) or on an object of unknown
origin is not reported.

`reads-environment` needs no targets. The ecosystem catalog tags these calls: `os.getenv`,
`os.getenvb`, the functions of `platform` that describe the machine or the interpreter
(`platform.system`, `platform.machine`, `platform.python_version`, ...),
`importlib.util.find_spec`, `importlib.import_module`, `importlib.metadata.version`,
`importlib.metadata.distribution`, `shutil.which`, and `sysconfig.get_config_var`; and these
reads: `os.environ`, `os.environb`, `os.name`, `sys.platform`, `sys.version`,
`sys.version_info`, `sys.hexversion`, `sys.implementation`, and `sys.flags`. An entry set
`excluded = true` (`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`, below) is never reported. A call on
`os.environ` (`os.environ.get("X")`) is a read of `os.environ`. One report per scope function
names the first read it reaches and counts every one.

`importlib.import_module(name, package)` and `importlib.util.find_spec(name, package)` read the
environment unless the module they import is established to be the project's own:

- every text `name` may hold names a module of the project (`"pkg.config"`, a module constant,
  either of two such texts) that the import finds in the project, or starts with a package of
  the project and a dot (`f"pkg.parser.{name}"`, `"pkg.parser." + name`, `"pkg.%s" % name`)
  under which it finds only modules of the project (below);
- a relative name (`".config"`, `f"..parser.{name}"`) is anchored at `package`: a text the code
  fixes, or the module's own `__package__` or `__name__`;
- the call is not inside a `try` with an `except` clause naming `ImportError` or
  `ModuleNotFoundError`: the code expects the import to fail.

Python finds the modules under a package on its `__path__`, the package's own directory unless
code changes it. heki follows what the modules of the project do to the `__path__` of a package,
its own in its `__init__.py` or another's through an import (`plugins.__path__`, `from plugins
import __path__`):

- adding directories after the package's own (`__path__.append(d)`, `__path__.extend(ds)`,
  `__path__ += ds`, `__path__ = __path__ + ds`, `__path__ = pkgutil.extend_path(__path__,
  __name__)`, also on `__import__("pkgutil")`, and `pkg_resources.declare_namespace`) leaves the
  package's own modules found first, but any other name under the package may be an installed
  module;
- any other change (`__path__ = [d]`, `__path__.insert(0, d)`, a slice store, `del __path__`), or
  a use heki does not follow (the list handed to a function other than a builtin that only reads
  it and `pkgutil.iter_modules`, `walk_packages`, or `extend_path`, returned, or stored
  elsewhere), may take any name under the package elsewhere, its own modules included. So may a
  package whose `__init__.py` heki cannot read.

Reading the path (iterating it, `__path__[0]`, `len(__path__)`, `pkgutil.iter_modules(__path__)`)
changes nothing. A module is found in the project when each package along its name leads the
import there first: heki takes the project's top-level packages to be found in the project, a
regular package of the project is found before the directories added after its parent's own,
and a directory without `__init__.py` is a namespace package with a portion in each directory of
its parent's path, in that order. A name under a package holds only modules of the project when
the packages along it lead to the project's directories alone and no package under it changes
its path: `f"pkg.{name}"` reads the environment once a package anywhere under `pkg` changes its
`__path__`, while a change in another package does not affect it.

A name heki cannot tell (a parameter, `"pkg" + name`, a namespace package without
`__init__.py`) stays a read of the environment, and so does an import of a module the project
does not have. A `call-targets` entry naming `importlib.import_module` matches every call of it.

- Each scope function is checked through any number of calls.
- A module body, what runs when the module is imported, is checked only where a scope names
  `<module>` itself: `pkg.gen:<module>` (the body of `pkg.gen`), `pkg.*:<module>` (of every
  module under `pkg`), `pkg.gen.<module>`, or `<module>` (of every module). `pkg.*` and
  `pkg.gen:*` keep naming the functions only. The body is checked as a scope function is (its
  module-level reads, calls, import probes, and writes), and the bodies of its classes, which
  run with it, count for what they take from outside the project (environment reads, import
  probes, and the external `call-targets` and `read-targets`), not for their other effects.
  Reports name it `<module>`.
- A violation inside another scope function is reported there only, once.
- One report per scope function and forbidden kind (or target) stands for every distinct site of
  it that the function reaches.

### `readonly-returns`

```toml
[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]
name = "schema-graph"
producers = ["pkg.parser.SchemaGraphBuilder.schema"]
deep = true
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name. |
| `producers` | `[]` | Functions, methods, external symbols, or attributes (`Class.attr`) whose result every caller shares. |
| `deep` | `false` | Protect the values below the result too: its attributes, items, and elements. |

- Functions decorated with `@lru_cache` / `@cache` are protected without configuration, also
  through an import alias, but not a `cache` decorator the module defines itself.
- Every function that returns a protected value, or a part of it, on some path is protected too:
  wrappers and property getters need no entry of their own.

### `invalidation`

```toml
[[tool.heki.invalidation]]
name = "graph-index"
targets = ["DataType.data_types", "DataModel.fields"]
invalidators = ["GenerationStore.note_changed_models", "GenerationStore.refresh_now"]
exempt-writers = ["pkg.parser.generation.*"]
message = "tell the store which models changed"
```

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | ------- | ------- |
| `name` | `""` | The contract's name in reports. |
| `targets` | `[]` | `Class.attr` attributes whose writes must be announced. |
| `invalidators` | `[]` | Functions or methods whose call announces the change. |
| `exempt-writers` | `[]` | Functions whose writes need no announcement of their own: the owner's operations, which announce or batch the change themselves, and construction methods. |
| `message` | none | The help of every report of the contract. |

An invalidator call counts when it runs on every path from the write to the function's normal
return:

- directly, or in each branch;
- behind a boolean flag the path sets after the write;
- through a helper that calls one on every path of its own.

What needs no announcement:

- a path that ends by raising: only normal returns count;
- writes to objects that did not exist before the call: an initializer's own `self` (not the
  objects reached through its attributes), and objects the function constructs or copies;
- writes to objects the function gets from a call;
- a function whose every caller announces the change after calling it.

A write is followed through local aliases (also in the scopes nested in the function),
container methods, `setattr` / `__dict__`, and helpers. A helper changing an argument it does
not type writes the field or instance its caller binds to it. At most 64 `invalidation`
contracts can be declared.

### How contracts report

These hold for `write-owners`, `read-owners`, and `call-owners`, and the reporting at callers
holds for `invalidation` too:

- **A class's own initialization is allowed.** An initializer (`__init__`, `__post_init__`,
  `__new__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`) of a target class or a subclass may access its own
  `self`: directly, through `super().__init__()`, or through helpers it passes `self` to.
- **A function that only runs inside allowed functions is allowed.** Every path of project
  callers above it starts in an allowed function, an exempt method, or such an initialization.
- **A private helper reports at its callers.** An access in a private helper (`_name`) with
  project callers is reported at the call sites of its first non-private callers. A private
  function called only by its own recursion reports its accesses itself.
- **`attribution = "lexical"` judges the code where it is written.** The two rules above do not
  apply: an access is judged in the function whose code holds it, whoever calls that function.
  A lambda, comprehension, or generator expression is part of the function it is written in, a
  class body's code part of the function running the class statement, and a nested `def` a
  function of its own. For `write-owners`, a call handing a typed object to a helper that
  changes it without knowing its class is the caller's write. With `unresolved = "report"`, the
  callers binding a parameter only tell its object's class, allowed callers included. A class's
  own initialization stays allowed, a helper it passes `self` to included when every path of
  project callers above the helper starts in such an initialization; so do `exempt-methods`,
  `fresh-objects`, and the targets of a call contract calling each other. Effect boundaries have
  no such key: they judge what their scope functions reach through any number of calls.
- **`own-receiver = "allow"` allows the accesses through a method's own receiver.** An access is
  allowed when the function it is judged in (the function reported, or with `attribution =
  "lexical"` the function holding the access) is a method that is no static method, and the
  object the member is looked up on may be its first parameter: `self._cache[k] = v`,
  `self._seen`, `cls._kind()`, `super()._label()`, `self._norm(x)` of a static method,
  `Resolver._label(self)`. A member the class inherits counts like its own. Another parameter, an
  attribute of the receiver, a static method called through its class, the parameter of a static
  method or of a function, and a nested `def`, lambda, or comprehension using the enclosing
  method's `self` (heki does not tie a variable a nested scope captures to the enclosing
  function's parameter) stay reported. By the call graph, a private helper the method hands its
  `self` (`_count(self)`) is judged at the method, and is allowed with it.
- **`allowed-protocols` allows the accesses through the protocols it names.** A read, call, or
  write through a value typed with a project protocol a pattern names (or a subprotocol of one)
  that declares the member, itself or through its protocol bases, is allowed wherever it is
  judged, and so is a reference that `references` counts (`return h._helper`): `allowed-protocols = ["*Host"]` allows `parser._flag` with `parser: RenderHost` and
  `class RenderHost(RuntimeFlags, Protocol)` when `RuntimeFlags` declares `_flag`, while the same
  read through `flags: RuntimeFlags` stays reported. A write through the protocol is allowed for
  the protocol's member and for each implementation's attribute alike. Accesses through a
  protocol that does not declare the member, through an implementation's class, through a value
  of unknown class (`unresolved = "report"`, also a protocol whose implementations heki cannot
  list), and a protocol-typed value handed to a helper that changes it without typing its
  parameter stay reported. By the call graph, a private method of an implementation that a call
  through the protocol runs still hands its writes of its own `self` to the caller.
- **One report stands for every site behind it.** A report at a call stands for every access
  behind the call, and an effect boundary's report for every site its scope function reaches.
  JSON output gives their number as `sites`, and a
  [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) counts each of them.

## Ecosystem knowledge: `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`

heki ships a catalog of blocking, async-safe, and offloading APIs of the standard library and
common packages (`requests`, `httpx`, `aiohttp`, `sqlalchemy`, `django`, `redis`, `pandas`, …).
Add your own or override an entry:

```toml
[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]
symbol = "mypkg.db.run_query"
effects = ["blocking_db", "db_query"]

[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]
symbol = "mypkg.workers.in_thread"
offloads-blocking-arg = 0     # calls its first argument on a thread
async-safe = true

[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]
symbol = "mypkg.logging.emit"
excluded = true               # never reported
```

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | ------- |
| `symbol` | Fully qualified function or method name (`package.module.Class.method`). |
| `effects` | Any of `blocking_net`, `blocking_db`, `blocking_subprocess`, `blocking_sync`, `sleep`, `blocking_fs`, `unpooled_client_alloc`, `db_query`, `quadratic_realloc`. |
| `async-safe` | Safe to call from `async def`: it never blocks the event loop, so the blocking effects in `effects` are ignored (`db_query` and `unpooled_client_alloc` still count in loops). |
| `offloads-blocking-arg` | Index of the callable argument this function runs on another thread (the receiver is not counted). |
| `excluded` | Never reported (logging and similar). |
| `copy-sanitizer` | Returns a copy of its first argument (or receiver), ending `MUT202` protection: `"deep"` copies everything below it too; `"shallow"` (or `true`) copies only the object itself, so the values below it stay protected. |
| `return-type` | The class of the objects the call returns (a factory: `mypkg.db.open` returning `sqlite3.Connection`), whose methods are then looked up in the catalog. |
| `sync-lock-or-tx` | A `with` over an instance of this class, or over the result of this call, holds a synchronous lock or a database transaction (`EFF106`). |
| `non-reentrant-lock` | An instance of this class is a lock its holder cannot take again: acquiring it while the same thread or task holds it waits forever (`EFF109`). |
| `one-at-a-time` | Tasks may not be inside this method on one object at once (`EFF110`): `"always"` (a second task's call raises), `"when_unbound"` (only while the object holds no connection, as an `AsyncSession`), or `"unbinds"` (as `"when_unbound"`, and the object holds no connection after the call: `commit`). |

- An override sets the keys it lists on the built-in entry for the same symbol. The keys it leaves
  out keep their built-in values; `effects = []` removes every effect.
- An entry may name a function or method of the project, by the module that defines it (the
  built-in catalog never describes the project's own functions).

For a project function:

| Key | Effect |
| --- | ------ |
| `effects` | added to what heki finds in its body |
| `excluded` | keeps every effect of the body from its callers |
| `async-safe` | keeps the blocking effects of the body from its callers |
| `return-type` | types its result, over its annotation |
| `offloads-blocking-arg` | the parameter the body offloads, counted as for a library method |
| `copy-sanitizer`, `sync-lock-or-tx`, `non-reentrant-lock`, `one-at-a-time` | not read: library symbols only |

## Inline suppressions

```python
x = load()            # heki: ignore[EFF101]
y = load()            # heki: ignore[EFF101, async-blocking-call]
z = load()            # heki: ignore
w = load()            # noqa: EFF101
```

- A suppression applies to the line of the diagnostic.
- Codes and rule names are accepted.
- A comment without codes (`# heki: ignore`, `# noqa`) silences every rule on that line.
- A bracketed list that is not closed or names no rule (`# heki: ignore[`, `# heki: ignore[]`)
  silences nothing.
- To keep a rule away from whole files, use [`per-file-ignores`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/

# Fixes and Safety

`heki check --fix` rewrites an `OPT` finding only when heki proves that the rewrite keeps what
the program does. This page shows the fix commands, what each finding offers, and what a fix
must prove.

## Fix commands

```console
$ heki check --diff                              # preview (exit code 1 when something would change)
$ heki check --fix                               # apply safe, unconditional fixes
$ heki check --fix --include-size-dependent      # also the proven-safe size-dependent rewrites
$ heki check --fix --profile profile.txt         # size-dependent rewrites in hot functions only
```

- A fix comes with a report: `--fix` applies only the fixes of the reports shown. A report whose
  rewrite heki proves safe is [exact](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications) and shown by default, so a
  run without configuration applies the fixes of `OPT101` and `OPT102`.
- `--diff` takes the same flags as `--fix` and writes nothing.
- `--include-size-dependent` applies the size-dependent rewrites in every function, with or
  without `--profile`.
- `--profile` alone applies them only in the functions a [profile](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#profiles) shows hot.

## What each finding offers

Every `OPT` rule finds a quadratic or linear-per-iteration pattern that has a faster equivalent.
Two independent questions decide whether heki offers the rewrite:

| Question | Possible answers |
| -------- | ---------------- |
| **Safety:** does the rewrite keep the program's behavior? | every proof obligation is `Established`, `Blocked` (cannot be proven here), or `Disproved` (a concrete counterexample shape exists) |
| **Profitability:** is the rewrite faster for every input? | unconditional, or size-dependent (it can be slower for tiny inputs or for loops that run zero times) |

### Safety

| Obligations | What you get |
| ----------- | ------------ |
| All established | A diagnostic with a fix. A statement whose shape heki does not rewrite (a parenthesized `x = (x + [i])`, an annotated `x: list = x + [i]`) gets a diagnostic saying the rewrite is proven safe, to be made by hand. |
| One blocked | A diagnostic naming the first blocking obligation, and no fix. |
| One disproved | Nothing: the pattern only looks quadratic, and rewriting it would be a bug. |

### Profitability

| Profitability | Rules | Certainty | Applied by |
| ------------- | ----- | --------- | ---------- |
| Unconditional (faster from the first iteration) | `OPT101`, `OPT102` | exact (the proven reports) | `heki check --fix` |
| Size-dependent | `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130` | exact (the proven reports) | `heki check --fix --include-size-dependent`, or `--fix --profile <dump>` in hot functions |
| Size-dependent, no rewrite | `OPT103`, `OPT112`, `OPT113` | `OPT103` exact (the proven reports), `OPT113` exact (its exact tier), `OPT112` heuristic | none: suggestion only |

### When the size is fixed

A size-dependent rule reports nothing when the code fixes the size:

- the container holds at most 16 items and nothing grows it past that or lets it escape. It
  is a display without `*` / `**` unpacking, a string constant, a builtin constructor of an
  iterable the code fixes (`list(range(7))`, `tuple(".;:")`, `sorted(NAMES)`, `list()`), a
  slice with constant bounds (`cases[:3]`, `paths[-2:]`), or a comprehension over fixed
  iterables (`[c for c in LABELS if c in wanted]`). Shrinking it (`expected.pop(0)` on
  `expected = [b"a", b""]`) and read-only builtins are fine, and so is filling a new list a
  fixed number of times (`ids.append(card["id"])` in a loop over at most 6 cards). A tuple or
  a string stays fixed whatever other code does with it, unless other code rebinds its name
  (`cfg.STATEMENTS = tuple(rows)`). This holds also through local names,
  module constants, and other modules' module-level displays and class attributes, read in a
  function or in a module body;
- the loop runs a fixed number of times: over such a container, a `range` of constants with at
  most 16 steps, or an iterable a test on every path to the loop caps (`if not 1 <= len(cards)
  <= 6: raise ValueError(...)`, `assert len(xs) <= 3`, also after a loop that shrinks it, when
  nothing on the way to the loop grows it or hands it to other code);
- the list is rebuilt in every iteration;
- the loop's own test caps the accumulator: `while len(buf) < 10`.

These facts decide profitability only, never safety. A size known only at run time does not
count: a list whose size depends on the input is reported even when it always holds three items.

## What a fix must prove

The analysis behind the `OPT` rules is separate from the one behind the other rules, and
deliberately conservative:

| Obligation | Why | Example |
| ---------- | --- | ------- |
| No type annotation is trusted | a subclass can override `__contains__` or `__add__` | `x: list[int] = WeirdList(...)` is not a list for heki |
| The object is created in the function and never escapes | heki counts anything it cannot see as shared: parameters, globals, attributes, values passed to unknown functions, names captured by closures | `sink(rows)` inside the loop blocks `rows.append(...)` |
| Access is exclusive: no other variable, iterator, or view still refers to the old object after the statement | an in-place update would change what they see | `for v in x: x = x + [v]` ends, but `x.append(v)` would loop forever, so heki reports nothing |
| Evaluation order and exceptions are kept | a rewrite must not call anything earlier or later | `{**d, f(): g()}` becomes `d.update({f(): g()})`, not `d[f()] = g()`, which would call `g` first |
| Builtin names are the builtins | the module can rebind them | trusted only while nothing rebinds them: an assignment, a `global` store, `from m import *`, any call of `globals()`, or a module that patches `builtins` (a `.pyi` stub never runs, so its `import builtins` does not count) |
| Locals change only through the code | `eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, `sys._getframe`, and frame attributes can change them behind any analysis | candidates in such functions are always blocked; `heki assumptions` lists these places in a project |

The scope analysis is checked against CPython's `symtable`, and adversarial programs that break a
naive rewrite are run on CPython: see [Development](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/development/#checks-against-cpython).

## How `--fix` applies fixes

1. It applies the fixes that do not overlap.
2. It analyzes the result again and repeats until nothing changes, at most ten passes: a fix that
   becomes provable after another one is applied too.
3. It reports what is left.

| Case | What happens |
| ---- | ------------ |
| A suppressed diagnostic (`# heki: ignore[...]`) | It is never fixed. |
| A file that changed on disk meanwhile (an editor saved it) | It is not written: the run keeps that save, reports an error, and exits with code 2. Run `--fix` again. |
| Fixes of a pass that would leave a file that does not parse | None of them is applied to that file, and the run exits with code 2 (a heki bug to report). |
| `\n`, `\r\n`, or lone `\r` line breaks | Fixes work the same, and the lines they insert use the file's own line break. |

`--diff` prints the paths every other output format prints (relative to the working directory),
so `patch -p1` applies it where heki ran.

## Fixes keep type checkers and isort satisfied

A `collections.deque` rewrite (`OPT120`, `OPT121`) also rewrites the variable's annotation and
adds the import:

```console
$ heki check --diff --include-size-dependent jobs.py
--- a/jobs.py
+++ b/jobs.py
@@ -1,11 +1,12 @@
 """Job queue."""
 
+import collections
 import os
 
 
 def drain(jobs: list[int]) -> int:
-    queue: list[int] = list(jobs)
+    queue: collections.deque[int] = collections.deque(list(jobs))
     total = 0
     while queue:
-        total += queue.pop(0)
+        total += queue.popleft()
     return total
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

- An annotation the fix cannot rewrite (`Sequence[int]`, a union), or another annotated
  declaration of the variable, blocks the fix.
- `import collections` goes into the module's block of standard-library imports, in the order
  that block follows: straight imports first, or sorted by module as with
  `force-sort-within-sections`.
- Without such a block, it starts one before the other imports. In a module without imports, it
  follows the docstring and `__future__` imports, with the blank lines isort expects.
- It never goes above a shebang, an encoding declaration, or a `from __future__` import, and only
  imports run before it, so the rewritten function cannot run before `collections` is bound.
- An existing `from collections import deque` or `import collections` is reused only when it runs
  unconditionally (not under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`), nothing else binds or deletes the name (no
  other store, no `del` in a function declaring it `global`, no star import that may rebind it),
  and it names the standard library's module (not `from .collections import deque`).

## Profiles

`--profile` reads a sampling profile you recorded offline. It is experimental; see [experimental.md](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

| Profiler | Command |
| -------- | ------- |
| CPython 3.15's sampling profiler | `python -m profiling.sampling run --collapsed -o stacks.txt app.py`, or `--gecko -o profile.json` |
| py-spy | `py-spy record --format raw -o stacks.txt -- python app.py` |

- A function is hot when it is on the stack in at least 1 % of the samples.
- The profile promotes size-dependent fixes in hot functions and adds the sample share to the
  diagnostics' evidence. It never makes an unsafe rewrite safe.

A frame counts for a function when all of these hold:

- its name names the function on a dotted boundary: `run` or `A.run` for `A.run`, never `BA.run`;
- its file is the function's file, as a basename, a relative path, or an absolute path;
- its line, when the profiler recorded one, lies inside the function.

A frame that fits several functions counts for none: a plain `run` without a line in a file with
two `run` methods, or a `models.py` that two packages have. `--watch` matches frames by their
names only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/

# Adopting heki in a Code Base

An existing code base usually has findings you cannot fix at once. This page shows how to adopt
heki step by step:

1. Record today's findings in a [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines), so heki fails only on
   new ones.
2. Run it in [pre-commit](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#pre-commit) and [continuous integration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#continuous-integration).
3. [Roll out more rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#rolling-out-rules): contracts for your shared state, and the opt-in
   rules where they matter.
4. For a library, save [effect snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103) of its public functions.

## Ratchet baselines

A Ratchet baseline records the findings you have today and fails only on new ones:

```console
$ heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml --update-baseline   # record today's findings
$ heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml                     # fail on regressions only
```

Set `baseline = "heki-baseline.toml"` in the [configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings)
to use it without the flag, also in `--watch` and the language server.

Entries are keyed by file, function, rule, and target, not by line number, so unrelated edits and
reformatting do not break the baseline:

```toml
# heki Ratchet baseline: counts may only shrink (`heki check --update-baseline`).
version = 2

[[entries]]
path = "app/api.py"
qualname = "get_user"
rule_code = "EFF101"
target = "requests.get"
count = 1
```

The recorded set can only shrink:

| Situation | `heki check` | `heki check --update-baseline` |
| --------- | ------------ | ------------------------------ |
| No baseline file yet | an error (exit code 2) | records today's findings |
| A finding was fixed | a note that the entry can shrink | records the smaller entry |
| An entry grew, or a new finding appeared | reports it, with a note on the allowed and found counts (exit code 1 for an error, and for a warning with [`fail-on = "warning"`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint)) | reports it the same way and leaves the file as it is (exit code 1) |
| A file could not be analyzed (a syntax error, an unreadable file) | reports the error and the other files' findings (exit code 2) | writes nothing, so the entries of that file are not lost (exit code 2) |

To record new findings on purpose, delete the baseline and record it again.

### What an entry counts

Each entry counts violation sites, not reports (`sites` in JSON output):

- a contract report at the caller of a private helper stands for every write, read, or call
  inside the helper;
- an effect boundary report stands for every forbidden call or write its scope function reaches.

So a second violation behind a recorded report is a regression too.

A baseline without `version = 2` was written before heki counted sites, and counts reports:

- `heki check` says so in a note, and a second site behind a recorded report is no regression;
- `--update-baseline` compares in the old unit first, so nothing that grew is taken in, then
  rewrites the file with `version = 2`.

A version this heki does not know is an error, and so is a file listing one entry twice (a hand
merge of two baselines).

## pre-commit

heki's checks follow calls across files, so the hook checks the whole project instead of the
staged files only:

```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki
    rev: v0.2.2
    hooks:
      - id: heki
```

The first run builds heki from the source of that release: pre-commit installs the repository as
a Python package, which maturin compiles with cargo (Rust 1.99 or newer; when cargo is not on
`PATH`, the build installs Rust into a cache directory first). That takes a few minutes, and
pre-commit keeps the installed hook for later runs. `pre-commit autoupdate` moves `rev` to the
latest release.

heki also ships as one binary on PyPI, so a local hook can run it without a compile or a Rust
toolchain:

=== "uv"

    ```yaml
    # .pre-commit-config.yaml
    repos:
      - repo: local
        hooks:
          - id: heki
            name: heki
            entry: uvx heki check
            language: system   # needs uv on PATH
            types: [python]
            pass_filenames: false
    ```

=== "Without uv"

    ```yaml
    # .pre-commit-config.yaml
    repos:
      - repo: local
        hooks:
          - id: heki
            name: heki
            entry: heki check
            language: python
            additional_dependencies: [heki]
            types: [python]
            pass_filenames: false
    ```

The hook fails on errors and passes with warnings, which it prints. To make warnings fail it too,
set `fail-on = "warning"` in `[tool.heki.lint]`, or add `--fail-on warning` to `entry`. With a
baseline configured, the hook fails only on new findings.

## Continuous integration

=== "GitHub Actions annotations"

    ```yaml
    - run: uvx heki check --output-format github
    ```

=== "Code scanning (SARIF)"

    ```yaml
    # The job needs `permissions: security-events: write`.
    - run: uvx heki check --output-format sarif > heki.sarif || test "$?" -eq 1
    - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
      with:
        sarif_file: heki.sarif
    ```

Warnings become annotations without failing the step; `fail-on = "warning"` in
`[tool.heki.lint]` (or `--fail-on warning`) makes them fail it, as in pre-commit.

With SARIF:

- findings become code-scanning alerts, warnings included, and keep the step green (exit code
  `1` when one fails the run);
- a configuration, read, or syntax error (exit code `2`) still fails the step; a file heki could
  not read or parse is an `error` notification of the run
  (`invocations[0].toolExecutionNotifications`, with `executionSuccessful: false`), and the
  results of the other files are kept;
- results carry the message, the location, the call chain (`relatedLocations`), and the help
  (`properties.help`; SARIF's `rules[].help` is one text per rule, and a report's help can name
  the object it is about).

For custom tooling, `--output-format json` gives every field: see
[Coding Agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#after-an-edit-heki-check).

## Rolling out rules

1. Start with the default rules and a baseline, or `--select` one family at a time. Only the
   exact rules run by default; add the heuristic ones with `lint.heuristic = true` (or
   `--heuristic`), or name the ones you want in `extend-select`. Their reports can be wrong
   about the code, and every output labels them `heuristic`
   ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).
2. Declare [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) for the shared state and the operations you
   care about, and effect boundaries for the code that must stay pure. `MUT201`, `MUT203`,
   `MUT204`, `MUT109`, and `EFF201` report nothing until a contract exists.
3. Enable the opt-in rules where they matter:

    | Rule | Certainty | Turn it on for |
    | ---- | --------- | -------------- |
    | [`EFF105`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/), [`EFF107`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | heuristic | async services |
    | [`EFF106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/) | heuristic | threaded code, and code that holds database transactions |
    | [`MUT103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/) | heuristic | library APIs (with [effect snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103)) |
    | [`MUT106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/) | heuristic | code that passes iterators and generators around |
    | [`MUT108`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | heuristic | code that relies on frozen dataclasses and `ReadOnly` fields |

4. Use `per-file-ignores` rather than broad `ignore` lists, so new code stays covered.

### From heki 0.1

heki 0.1 ran every rule that is not opt-in by default. Since rules have a certainty, only the
exact ones do: in 0.2.0, `EFF101`, `EFF103`, `DATA101`, the proven tier of the eight `OPT`
rewrite rules (`OPT101`-`OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`), their
reports whose rewrite heki proves safe, and the exact tier of `OPT113` ([Rule
precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications) lists them).

- `lint.heuristic = true` restores the rules of 0.1, now labelled `heuristic` in every output.
- A baseline keeps its entries: their keys (file, function, rule, target) do not change.
- `heki check --fix` applies the proven fixes of `OPT101` and `OPT102` by default, as in 0.1.

## Effect snapshots (`MUT103`)

For a library, a change in what a public function *does* is worth reviewing even when no rule
fires: it starts mutating an argument, or doing network I/O. Save the effect summaries of the
public functions and check against them:

```console
$ heki snapshot --write                        # writes .heki-summary-snapshot.json
$ heki check --extend-select MUT103            # reports functions that gained effects
```

1. Commit `.heki-summary-snapshot.json`.
2. When a new effect is intended, refresh the snapshot in the same pull request: the diff of the
   JSON file shows reviewers what changed.

A run that cannot analyze every file (a syntax error, an unreadable file) does not write the
snapshot: it reports the errors and exits with code 2, so the entries of those files are not
lost.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/

# Configuration Advice

!!! warning "Experimental"

    `heki recommend` is experimental: what it prints, its policies, and its JSON object can
    still change in any release. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

`heki recommend` analyzes a project as `heki check` does and prints advice on its
configuration, with counts from the project and the keys to add to `[tool.heki]`. It writes no
file and runs none of the project's code.

```console
$ heki recommend
$ heki recommend app --output-format json
```

It takes the options of `heki check` that decide what is analyzed: `--select`,
`--extend-select`, `--ignore`, `--heuristic` / `--no-heuristic`, `--config`,
`--target-version`, and `--baseline`. The advice is relative to that configuration.

## What it prints

- **The project**: the root, and the files and functions analyzed.
- **Reports now**: what `heki check` prints with the configuration, as exact and heuristic
  reports (reports sharing a root cause count once, as `heki check` folds them), the heuristic
  reports of exact rules that `lint.heuristic = false` withholds, and the heuristic rules it
  leaves off. With a baseline, the reports it allows and the regressions.
- **Rules worth enabling here**: every rule the configuration leaves off, and every exact rule
  whose heuristic reports it withholds, with the reports naming it in `extend-select` would add
  (exact and heuristic, and with a baseline the regressions among them), its consequence, and
  the published measurement of how often its reports are right about the code
  ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)), or "not measured". Rules without reports here are named on
  one line.
- **Contract candidates**: the `write-owners`, `read-owners`, and `effect-boundaries`
  contracts the code already keeps, each with its confidence and evidence, and the trial run of
  its rules that verified it; then the candidates a trial rejected, with the report it made.
- **Notes**: what to know to weigh the advice. When the paths given leave out Python files
  below the project root, the note names them: heki takes the files it analyzed as the whole
  project, so what it says about callers, readers, and writers holds for those files only. It
  counts up to 50 such files, among the first 10,000 entries below the root.
- **The keys to add or change**, for the file the project reads its configuration from:
  `[tool.heki...]` tables in a `pyproject.toml`, tables at the top level in `heki.toml`,
  `.heki.toml`, or a `--config` file. Without a configuration file, the keys go into a new
  `pyproject.toml`. The block only adds: an array the file already sets is written whole, with
  the additions named in a comment, since TOML cannot append to an array.

## Which rules the block enables

A rule enters the block when it reports here, is not experimental, reports bugs (its severity
is `error`), and no published measurement shows real harm below 10%. The other rules are
listed with the reason they stay out:

- slower code, and bugs that are rarely harmful, are worth reading but not worth failing a run
  for;
- experimental rules are listed apart, under "Optional", and never enabled;
- a rule the configuration ignores stays ignored;
- `MUT103` compares with a summary snapshot you save with `heki snapshot --write`;
- contract rules run when their contract is declared, so they are not listed here.

## Which contracts the block declares

Candidates are drawn from what the code does, never from names:

- `write-owners`: an attribute of a project class written after its object is constructed only
  by functions of one module, and read in at least two other modules. The entry allows the
  smallest of `module:Class.*` and `module:*` that covers the writers. An attribute written
  only while its objects are constructed (by an initializer, or by a function filling the object
  it constructs) gets an entry that allows no writer.
- `read-owners`: a private attribute (`_name`) read only by functions of its class's module,
  whose class is used in at least two modules. The entry allows the readers as above.
- `effect-boundaries`: a module whose functions reach no blocking call, with
  `forbid = ["blocking"]`; a package whose every module qualifies is one scope. A scope has at
  least three functions. Test code, as `relax-async-in-tests` finds it, gets no boundary.

What the configuration already declares is not proposed: an attribute a `write-owners` or
`read-owners` target names, and a module an effect boundary forbidding every blocking effect
covers. A kind whose rule the configuration ignores is not proposed either. Each target has the
module-part form (`app.models:Order.items`), which never matches another project's names.

The contract trial declares every candidate at once, the ownership contracts with
`unresolved = "report"`, and runs their rules (`MUT201` and `MUT205`, `MUT203` and `MUT206`,
`EFF201`) as `heki check` would: inline suppressions and `per-file-ignores` apply, and the
reports they drop are counted apart. A candidate its rule reports is rejected and listed with the
first report. Of each kind, the trial declares the first 32 candidates: `write-owners` with the
attributes changed in place first, then by the modules reading them; `read-owners` by the
modules using the class; boundaries by their functions times the functions calling into them
from outside. The configuration's own `write-owners` contracts count against the 32.

| Confidence | When |
| ---------- | ---- |
| high | the trial reports nothing for the contract, every Python file below the project root was analyzed, and no function of a boundary's scopes reaches code heki does not see (a call it does not resolve, a library name without a catalog entry, a function it does not model) |
| medium | the trial reports no violation, but `MUT205` or `MUT206` reports accesses on objects of unknown class (they are listed, and the entry sets `unresolved = "ignore"`), files were left out, or a scope function reaches code heki does not see (it is listed) |

Medium candidates are in the block too. A candidate on a subclass is left out when the one on
its base class is kept: a target covers the subclasses of its class. Every candidate carries the
caveat that accesses inside code heki cannot follow are not seen.

The verification run then applies the whole block, the rules it enables and the contracts it
declares, as `heki check` would; the counts of the block's rules come from it. A contract that
reports there is dropped, and the run repeats once.

## How the advice is kept honest

- Every count comes from the project, through the analysis `heki check` runs: inline
  suppressions, `per-file-ignores`, and the baseline apply as they do there. With the block
  applied, `heki check` prints the reports it promises.
- A contract enters the block only when a trial of its rules reports nothing on the code as it
  is, and a run with the whole block confirms it.
- How often a rule's reports are right is quoted only from published measurements, with their
  sample, interval, and date; a rule without one is "not measured". No score is computed.
- The same input, configuration, and heki version give the same report, on any machine and
  with any number of threads.
- It writes nothing and keeps every value the configuration sets.

[ADR-020](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md#adr-020-heki-recommend-advice-on-the-configuration-from-the-projects-own-analysis)
records these rules and the decisions behind the command.

## Example

A project with three modules and a test file:

```python
# app/users.py
import requests

def fetch_name(user_id: int) -> str:
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}", timeout=5).text

def load_user(user_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"id": str(user_id), "name": fetch_name(user_id)}

def known_names(names: list[str], source: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    known = list(source)
    found = []
    for name in names:
        if name in known:
            found.append(name)
    return found
```

```python
# app/report.py
def total_and_count(rows: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    items = (r for r in rows)
    total = sum(items)
    count = len(list(items))
    return total, count


def average(rows: list[int]) -> float:
    return sum(rows) / len(rows) if rows else 0.0


def spread(rows: list[int]) -> int:
    return max(rows) - min(rows) if rows else 0
```

```python
# app/api.py
from app.users import load_user

async def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    return load_user(user_id)
```

```python
# tests/test_users.py
def test_load_user() -> None:
    pass
```

```console
$ heki recommend app
heki recommend (experimental) on .: 3 file(s), 11 function(s)

Reports now  1 shown (1 exact, 0 heuristic), 1 heuristic withheld, 5 heuristic rule(s) off

Rules worth enabling here
  rule    reports  exact  consequence  right about the code (published)  real harm  block
  MUT106        1      -  bug          not measured                      -          yes
  OPT110        1      0  slowdown     78% (65-87%), n=50, 2026-11-21    6%         no: slower code, not a bug
  No reports here: EFF102, EFF105, EFF106, EFF107, EFF109, EFF110, EFF111, EFF113, MUT101, MUT107, MUT108, MUT111, MUT112, MUT113, MUT115, MUT118, OPT112
  MUT103: it compares with a saved summary snapshot: run `heki snapshot --write`, then select it.

Contract candidates
  effect-boundaries  app.report  medium
    3 function(s) in 1 module(s) reach no blocking call heki sees
    trial: EFF201 0
  For every candidate, accesses inside code heki cannot follow (unresolved calls, libraries without a catalog) are not seen.

Notes
  - 1 Python file(s) below the project root were not analyzed (tests/test_users.py): heki takes the analyzed files as the whole project, so what it says about callers, readers, and writers holds for those files only.

pyproject.toml: keys to add or change
  [tool.heki.lint]
  extend-select = ["MUT106"]  # adds MUT106

  [[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
  name = "app.report without blocking calls"
  scopes = ["app.report:*"]
  forbid = ["blocking"]
```

## JSON output

`--output-format json` prints one object, described by the JSON Schema at
[schemas/recommend-1.json](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/recommend-1.json), the URL its `$schema` field names, which
`heki recommend --output-format-json-schema` prints.
Within a `version`, fields are only added; the `version` changes when a field is removed or
changes meaning.

| Field | Content |
| ----- | ------- |
| `kind`, `version`, `heki` | `heki-recommend`, the version of the object, and the version of heki |
| `root`, `config_file`, `table_prefix` | the project root, the configuration file (`null` without one), and the table its keys are under (`tool.heki`, or empty) |
| `analyzed` | the files and functions analyzed, the files that could not be read or parsed, the paths given, and the Python files below the root they leave out |
| `runs` | the analyses the report was computed from: `discovery`, then `contract-trial` when there are candidates, and `verification` (with whether it `repeated`) when the block adds anything |
| `reports_now` | the counts of "Reports now" |
| `rules` | each rule of "Rules worth enabling here": its metadata, the reports it would add, its published measurement, whether the block enables it, and why |
| `contracts` | each contract candidate the block declares: its kind, what it is about, its entry, confidence, evidence, what the trial reported, and caveats |
| `rejected_contracts` | the candidates a run reported for, with the run and its reports |
| `contracts_not_tried` | per kind, the candidates past the first 32, which no trial declared |
| `notes` | the notes |
| `config`, `config_toml` | the keys to add or change, as keys and values and as TOML |
| `content` | the report as the text output prints it |

Exit codes: `0` the report was printed; `2` configuration, I/O, or syntax errors (the report
of the other files is still printed, as `heki check` does). It never exits with `1`: it checks
nothing.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/cli-reference/

# CLI Reference

Exit codes: `0` no diagnostic that fails the run (warnings are reported without failing it), `1` an `error` diagnostic, or a `warning` with `--fail-on warning` (`lint.fail-on`), among the Ratchet regressions when a baseline is used (or a refused `--update-baseline`, or pending `--diff` changes), `2` configuration / I/O / syntax errors.

A file that cannot be read or does not parse does not stop the run: `heki check` reports its error, checks and reports the other files, and exits with `2`, also when it reports diagnostics. A file that does not parse cannot run either, so nothing it would do is assumed; the names under its module resolve to nothing. SARIF output lists such files as `error` notifications of a run that did not execute successfully (`invocations[0].toolExecutionNotifications`, `executionSuccessful: false`); JSON output holds the diagnostics only.

## `heki`

```text
Experimental static checker for Python that tracks side effects and mutations across function calls

Usage: heki <COMMAND>

Commands:
  check        Run semantic checks across Python files or directories (Ruff-aligned)
  server       Start the incremental Language Server Protocol (LSP) server [alias: lsp]
  rule         Explain a rule, its Proof Obligations, and counterexamples (`ruff rule` style) [alias: explain]
  snapshot     Manage interprocedural effect summary snapshots (`MUT103`)
  assumptions  List Assumption A1 hazards (`eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, frame introspection, functions too large to model) in a project
  inspect      Experimental: what heki knows about one function (its effects, what it changes, keeps, and returns, whether it is pure, its callers, reports, and contracts)
  recommend    Experimental: advice on the configuration of a project, with counts from its analysis, and the keys to add (it writes no file)
  help         Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help     Print help
  -V, --version  Print version
```

## `heki check`

```text
Run semantic checks across Python files or directories (Ruff-aligned)

Usage: heki check [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [PATHS]...  Files or directories to check [default: .]

Options:
      --fix
          Apply `safe` + `unconditional` fixes (`OPT101`/`OPT102`)
      --include-size-dependent
          Also apply the proven-safe `size-dependent` fixes, in every function
      --diff
          Preview fixes as a unified diff without writing files
      --select <SELECT>
          Comma-separated rule codes, prefixes, or slugs to enable
      --extend-select <EXTEND_SELECT>
          Additional rules to enable on top of defaults/config
      --ignore <IGNORE>
          Comma-separated rule codes or slugs to ignore
      --heuristic
          Also run the heuristic rules, whose reports can be wrong about the code, by default and for every prefix and `ALL` (`lint.heuristic = true`)
      --no-heuristic
          Run a heuristic rule only when its code or name is selected (`lint.heuristic = false`)
      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`
      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`, `py312`, `py313`, `py314`, `py315`)
      --baseline <BASELINE>
          Ratchet baseline TOML file (line-number-independent)
      --fail-on <FAIL_ON>
          Exit with code 1 on reports of this severity or higher: `error` (the default), or `warning` to fail on warnings too (`lint.fail-on`) [possible values: error, warning]
      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>
          Output format [default: full] [possible values: full, concise, json, github, sarif]
      --color <WHEN>
          When to color the `full` and `concise` output and `--diff`, as Ruff does: `auto` colors them on a terminal unless `NO_COLOR` is set (`FORCE_COLOR` or `CLICOLOR_FORCE` color them anywhere), `always`, or `never` [default: auto] [possible values: auto, always, never]
      --update-baseline
          Generate or shrink-update the Ratchet baseline file
      --profile <PROFILE>
          Experimental: offline profile dump (collapsed stacks of CPython 3.15's profiler or py-spy, or `--gecko` JSON): apply the `size-dependent` fixes in its hot functions (in every function with `--include-size-dependent`)
      --watch
          Watch for file changes and re-run incrementally
      --generate-prompt [<QUESTION>]
          Experimental: print a prompt for consulting a language model about this run instead of the report: the configuration, the rules that apply, the diagnostics, how to answer, and QUESTION when given (put PATHS before the option). `--output-format json` prints it as JSON. Writes no file and exits with 0
      --output-format-json-schema <TARGET>
          Print the JSON Schema of a JSON output and exit: `generate-prompt`, the object of `--generate-prompt --output-format json` [possible values: generate-prompt]
  -h, --help
          Print help
```

## `heki server`

```text
Start the incremental Language Server Protocol (LSP) server

Usage: heki server [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --stdio         Use stdio transport (default LSP mode)
      --heuristic     Also run the heuristic rules, whose reports can be wrong about the code, by default and for every prefix and `ALL` (`lint.heuristic = true`)
      --no-heuristic  Run a heuristic rule only when its code or name is selected (`lint.heuristic = false`)
  -h, --help          Print help
```

## `heki rule`

```text
Explain a rule, its Proof Obligations, and counterexamples (`ruff rule` style)

Usage: heki rule [OPTIONS] [RULE]

Arguments:
  [RULE]  Rule code (`EFF101`) or slug (`async-blocking-call`), or `--all` to list all rules

Options:
      --all                            
      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>  `text`, or `json` with each rule's metadata and documentation [default: text] [possible values: text, json]
  -h, --help                           Print help
```

```text
          Write `.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root (default: print it)
      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`

          Target Python version (`py311`..`py315`)
  -h, --help
          Print help
```

# Rules

heki has 42 rules in four families. A rule is exact when it reports only what it established and was certified on the corpus, and heuristic (≈) when a report can be wrong about the code: [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/) says how a rule is certified and what each one measured. Each rule's page says what a report states.

- The exact rules run by default, and for a prefix such as `EFF` or `ALL`. A report of an exact rule that did not establish every premise (an `OPT` report whose rewrite is not proven) is shown where a heuristic rule would run.
- A heuristic rule runs when `select` / `extend-select` names its code or name. With `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`), the heuristic rules that are not opt-in also run by default and for a prefix or `ALL`.
- The opt-in rules marked 🔌 run only when `select` / `extend-select` names their exact code or name.
- The contract rules marked 📜 run when their contract is declared, whatever their certainty.

## Legend

- 🛠️ The fix is applied by `heki check --fix` when heki proves it safe.
- 🔧 A proven-safe rewrite applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` or in functions a `--profile` dump shows hot (it can be slower for tiny inputs).
- ≈ Heuristic rule: a report can be wrong about the code. Every output labels its reports `heuristic`.
- 🔌 Opt-in rule.
- 📜 Contract rule: it reports only what a declared contract asks for.
- 🧪 Experimental rule. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## Mutation & State (MUT)

Shared state written behind its owner's back: stale caches, write-ownership contracts, shared return values, and effect regressions against a saved snapshot.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| MUT101 | [cached-property-stale-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/) | Mutating an attribute read by `@cached_property` without invalidating the cache. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT103 | [summary-effect-regression](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/) | Interprocedural mutation/escape/effect regression against saved summary snapshot. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT106 | [iterator-double-consumption](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/) | Opt-in: consuming a single-pass iterator or generator a second time (the second pass sees no items). | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT107 | [hash-attr-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/hash-attr-mutation/) | Opt-in: a method other than the initializers rebinds or changes in place an attribute that the `__hash__` of its instances reads. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT108 | [readonly-type-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place a field that a standard type declares read-only (frozen dataclass / `NamedTuple` / `dataclass_transform` fields, `Final` / `ReadOnly` attributes, `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys), directly, through an alias, or in a helper. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT109 | [write-without-invalidation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-without-invalidation/) | Writing a declared `invalidation` target (directly, via alias, or via helper) without reaching one of its invalidators on every path to the function's return. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT110 | [readonly-param-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/) | Handing a `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `ReadOnly` parameter, as itself, to a function whose body (or a helper's) changes it in place at a named line. |  |
| MUT111 | [cached-property-stale-read](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/) | Opt-in: reading a `@cached_property` that a method of its class family can leave stale (a write `MUT101` reports). | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT112 | [conditional-ownership-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place a value that is a new object on one path and borrowed state (a parameter, an attribute, a global, or what a function returns of such state) on another. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT113 | [iterated-container-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/) | Opt-in: a dict, set, or deque of the instance changed while a method iterates it, by another method while a generator is suspended in the loop or by a function the loop's body calls (the next step raises `RuntimeError`). | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT114 | [cached-result-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/) | Changing in place the list, dict, or set that a `functools.lru_cache` / `functools.cache` function returned (the cache hands the same object to later calls with the same arguments), directly or through the functions that return it. |  |
| MUT115 | [shallow-copy-nested-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/shallow-copy-nested-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place an object below a shallow copy the function made of state that outlives the call (`dict(x)`, `x.copy()`, `copy.copy(x)`, `model_copy()`): the copied value holds the same object, so the change is seen through it too. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT118 | [sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy/) | `copy.deepcopy` of an instance holding an `object()` sentinel in an attribute that a function tests against the sentinel by identity (the copy holds a new object, which the test does not match). | ≈ |
| MUT201 | [write-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-owner-violation/) | Writing a guarded attribute/container (directly, via alias, or via helper) outside declared `write-owners`. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT202 | [readonly-return-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/) | Mutating a shared object returned by a declared `readonly-returns` producer, directly or through the functions that return it. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT203 | [read-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/) | Reading a guarded attribute (directly, via alias, `getattr`, or `__dict__`) outside declared `read-owners`. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT204 | [call-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/) | Calling a guarded function or method, or constructing a guarded class (directly, via a bound method, `getattr`, or a helper), outside declared `call-owners`. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT205 | [unresolved-guarded-write](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/) | Strict mode of a `write-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): writing an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class, or a computed attribute name on a guarded class. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT206 | [unresolved-guarded-read](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/) | Strict mode of a `read-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): reading an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT207 | [unresolved-guarded-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/) | Strict mode of a `call-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): calling a method named like a target on an object of unknown class. | ≈ 📜 |

## Execution Effects (EFF)

Work that runs where it should not: blocking calls on the event loop, clients and queries inside loops.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| EFF101 | [async-blocking-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/) | A call in `async def` that always runs a network, database, subprocess, or sleep call that waits on the event loop. |  |
| EFF111 | [async-possibly-blocking-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-possibly-blocking-call/) | Heuristic sibling of `EFF101`: a call in `async def` that can reach a blocking call on the event loop. | ≈ |
| EFF102 | [loop-unpooled-client](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/) | Allocating an unpooled HTTP/DB/RPC client or sessionless request inside a loop. | ≈ |
| EFF103 | [loop-db-query](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/) | A loop over data whose every iteration sends a database statement. |  |
| EFF113 | [loop-possible-db-query](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-possible-db-query/) | Heuristic sibling of `EFF103`: a loop that can run a database query on every iteration. | ≈ |
| EFF105 | [async-blocking-fs](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/) | Opt-in: blocking local filesystem I/O reachable from `async def`. | ≈ 🔌 |
| EFF106 | [lock-or-tx-held-across-io](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/) | Opt-in: `await` or blocking network I/O while holding a `threading` lock or a DB transaction. | ≈ 🔌 |
| EFF107 | [unretained-async-task](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | Opt-in: an `asyncio.create_task` result bound to a local variable but never awaited, returned, or stored. | ≈ 🔌 |
| EFF109 | [lock-reacquired-while-held](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-reacquired-while-held/) | Opt-in: a non-reentrant lock (`threading.Lock`, `asyncio.Lock`) taken again, directly or through a call, while it is held (the thread or task waits for itself). | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| EFF110 | [exclusive-object-fanout](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/exclusive-object-fanout/) | Opt-in: an object allowing one operation at a time (`asyncio.StreamReader`, an asyncpg connection, a WebSocket) used by tasks started together (`asyncio.gather`, a task group). | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| EFF201 | [effect-boundary-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/effect-boundary-violation/) | Reaching a forbidden effect (directly or through calls) from a declared `effect-boundaries` scope. | ≈ 📜 |

## Data Pipelines (DATA)

Quadratic re-allocation of DataFrames and arrays across loop iterations.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| DATA101 | [loop-carried-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/) | Loop-carried quadratic `pandas.concat` / `numpy.vstack` / `numpy.append` accumulation. |  |

## Complexity Rewrites (OPT)

Quadratic patterns heki can rewrite, each proven safe by the alias analysis before a fix is offered.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| OPT101 | [list-quadratic-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/) | Unconditionally profitable `list` quadratic concatenation (`x = x + [e]` -> `x.append(e)`). | 🛠️ |
| OPT102 | [set-dict-quadratic-merge](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-dict-quadratic-merge/) | Unconditionally profitable `set`/`dict` quadratic merge (`{**d, ...}` with `d` first). | 🛠️ |
| OPT103 | [immutable-quadratic-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/immutable-quadratic-concat/) | Size-dependent immutable quadratic accumulation (`bytes`/`tuple`/attr `str`). |  |
| OPT110 | [loop-linear-membership](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-membership/) | Size-dependent `e in lst` inside a loop -> hoist `set` outside loop. | 🔧 |
| OPT111 | [loop-linear-dedup](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-dedup/) | Size-dependent `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` -> auxiliary `set`. | 🔧 |
| OPT112 | [loop-linear-list-lookup](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-list-lookup/) | Size-dependent `list.index` / `list.remove` / `list.count` inside a loop (repeated linear scans). | ≈ |
| OPT113 | [nested-loop-equijoin](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/) | Size-dependent nested-loop equi-join (`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k`) -> `dict` index. |  |
| OPT120 | [list-front-pop](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-pop/) | Size-dependent `q.pop(0)` / `del q[0]` / `q = q[1:]` -> `collections.deque`. | 🔧 |
| OPT121 | [list-front-insert](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-insert/) | Size-dependent `q.insert(0, v)` -> `collections.deque`. | 🔧 |
| OPT130 | [loop-invariant-container-rebuild](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-invariant-container-rebuild/) | Size-dependent loop-invariant container reconstruction (`e in set(keys)`). | 🔧 |
